subtopic: GOVERNOR OF THE BANK OF CANADA
GOVERNOR OF THE BANK OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this morning we read in the newspapers that Canada's number one banker, the Governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Crow, has had annual salary increases ranging from 12 to 21 per cent since he was appointed in 1987, while the Canadian average was 4.5 per cent in 1988 and 5.25 per cent in 1989.
Nevertheless, Mr. Crow insists that a 5 per cent increase is inflationary. The government is taking steps to reduce the deficit and asking Canadians to help by tightening their belts. The salaries of the members of this House, Mr. Speaker, have increased by an average of only 2.8 per cent annually over the past six years.
Without wishing to question Mr. Crow's competence and credibility, I think he has a duty to practise what he preaches. This morning, Canadians were indignant, as I was, when they heard the news.
I hope Mr. Crow will be more consistent in the future and will take the necessary corrective action.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to rise in the House today to extend warm wishes to the Greek community in Canada as it recently celebrated, on March 25, the one hundred and sixty-ninth year of Greek independence.
This event stands as a proud testimony to the dynamism of the Greek people, their history and their culture. One hundred and sixty-nine years ago the Greek people ignited the first spark of a democratic movement as they fought for freedom against the Ottoman Empire. Since that time, the people of Greece and Greeks around the world have carried the torch of democracy proudly and with great dignity.
Almost daily we open our newspapers and read of sweeping political changes taking place all over the world. Everywhere the voice of democracy seems to be booming. However, it saddens me that while in other countries there is a general ease of tension, the situation in Cyprus has not changed. For the past 25 years Canada has had peacekeeping troops in Cyprus.
I strongly urge the government to apply whatever pressure possible to encourage demilitarization and dialogue so that democracy might once again be restored and Canadian troops can return home.

Mr. Speaker, last evening this House had the opportunity to pass a motion presented by my colleague from Mission-Coquitlam. The motion called on this government to negotiate with the provinces and develop a bill of rights for children. It would have given legal standing to the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child.
In debate, the government side expressed its genuine concern for the future of Canada's children. There were compassionate voices from that side of the House. But last night we witnessed the victory of partisanship over principle. Eighty-two government members voted against this motion. They turned and voted against a bill of rights for children.
Mr. Speaker, I am still shocked. This government denied Canadian children rights that we want for all the children of the world. To add insult to injury, the Prime Minister has agreed to co-chair the World Summit for Children. Such hypocrisy. The actions of this government yesterday show that it cares more about the

March 28, 1990
limelight of the international stage than the future of real children in Canada.
I want Canadians to know that we had a great opportunity to help all children and I want Canadians to know who ended that hope; it was the 82 members on the government side who voted against a bill of rights for children.

Mr. Speaker, this week marks the eleventh anniversary celebration of Children and Hospitals Week. Children and Hospitals Week is a public awareness campaign which focuses attention on the unique needs of children and family as they interact with the health care system. This year's theme is commitment to caring and a major goal of the week is to promote health care policies and practices which are both sensitive and responsive to the emotional and developmental needs of paediatric patients. Children and Hospitals Week is sponsored annually by the Association for the Care of Children's Health.
I invite all Canadians to celebrate Children and Hospitals Week by taking part in special events such as health fairs, hospital tours and, for the NDP, Teddy Bear clinics and balloon launches.
Finally, I applaud the Association for the Care of Children's Health and its members for their commitment to promoting the psychosocial well-being of children and families in health care settings.

Mr. Speaker, as the opposition critic for youth, I today want to salute a young lady from my riding who was named Miss Teen Canada.
Tonya Goss was a student of mine at Notre Dame High School just a few years ago. I recall a time when we were talking about the Parliament of Canada and studying Canadian history. She is now becoming a part of that by being named here in this House of Commons and saluted by all of us for her accomplishments.
She was an excellent student and an effervescent young lady who was not only captain but coach of the cheerleading team. I believe that Tonya Goss will not only represent the city of Welland well; she will represent the Niagara Peninsula and, indeed, all of Canada as she travels extensively both within Canada and without, representing us. She will be a fine ambassador and I do indeed salute her in all of our names.

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF THE BANK OF CANADA
GOVERNOR OF THE BANK OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today, Le Devoir reported that since 1986, the Governor of the Bank of Canada has had salary increases ranging from 12 to 21 per cent. Without wishing to question Mr. Crow's dedication, since we all know he is waging a tough battle against inflation, I think we should remember that the average Canadian has to make do with an annual increase of about 5.25 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is important that we keep things in perspective.

subtopic: GOVERNOR OF THE BANK OF CANADA
GOVERNOR OF THE BANK OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, was shocked to learn that the battle against inflation being waged by the Governor of the Bank of Canada does not extend to his own salary. I had fully expected that the man who asks so much from western Canadians would lead by example. Instead, I find that Mr. Crow has accepted wage increases of at least 12 per cent a year for the past several years and now the media reports a salary of up to $243,000.
How can we continue to ask the regions of this country to suffer today in order to have a better future tomorrow while at the same time Mr. Crow himself acts as as contributor to the inflation we are trying to control? I cannot justify these salary increases and I cannot ask my constituents to understand how this happens.
The newspaper headline reads: "Crow has no choice but to keep interest high". I will keep my interest high if Mr. Crow refuses his increase.
March 28, 1990

Mr. Speaker, one of the most unconscionable aspects of the finance minister's recent budget was the cuts to our veterans. Canadians realize that we must ensure that the surviving Canadian veterans, who fought to restore freedom to millions and to help change the history of the world for the better, should be given every consideration.
Yet this government has decided to show its respect by forcing many of our veterans in long-term chronic care to pay as much as 400 per cent more for board and lodging. This government has also reduced the Veterans Independence Program by $18 million. This program assisted those 60,000 veterans still living at home with housecleaning duties they can no longer maintain themselves.
As veteran Captain P. L. Bender from my riding of Nepean wrote: "Such a move is highly inconsiderate and thoughtless. There are not many veterans left and all young people should remember that the life they are enjoying today is due in some considerable degree to those who fought in the wars".
Our veterans deserve better. They have already paid their dues.

Mr. Speaker, the so-called campaign for fair taxes is a real con job being perpetrated on the public.
Unfair taxes are those which: (a) are hidden from consumers; (b) negatively impact on lower-income Canadians; (c) discriminate against Canadian goods in favour of imports; and (d) are applied at different levels to different things.
The GST does none of these things. It is an up-front, visible sales tax. The GST credit will shield lower-income Canadians who will end up better off under the GST than before. It removes the discrimination against locally produced goods, and it is applied uniformly to goods and services.
I believe in fair taxation, that is why I support the GST. That is why a vote against the GST is a vote against fan-taxes.

Mr. Speaker, the nominees for corporate welfare bum of the week are again three major corporations that did not pay any federal income taxes in 1988. They are: Brascan, Confederation Life Insurance and Xerox Canada. The three companies had combined profits of close to $400 million but did not contribute their fair share of taxes.
Were these companies so hard up that they could not contribute to their favour charities, the Liberal and Conservative Parties? Of course not. For instance, Xerox Canada gave over $11,000 to both the Liberals and the Conservatives.
And now for the winner. The envelope, please. And the winner is Brascan. Brascan is the corporate welfare bum of the week. It did not pay income taxes on profits of $263 million but it did give $50,000 to the Tories and $25,000 to the Liberals in 1988. Brascan did not forget to "dance with the one who brung ya".

Mr. Speaker, Canadian farmers are hurting right across Canada, from the wheat grower in the prairie provinces to the com producer in southwestern Ontario. Net farm incomes are the lowest in decades in many provinces. Farm bankruptcies have increased dramatically. In fact, in Saskatchewan, they have tripled in the last three years to 152 last year. Farm incomes are so low that at least one-quarter of the grain producers in Saskatchewan are facing the loss of their farms. Bankers will not give loans any more on the basis of equity, but purely on the basis of cash flow, and many grain prices are so low that the crops will not cash flow.
I call on the government to respond to this tragedy for tens of thousands of Canadian farm families and to provide emergency assistance now.

March 28, 1990
Oral Questions ROUGE RIVER VALLEY

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship); Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 26, the Ontario Government announced that over 10,500 acres of the Rouge River Valley System will be saved as a park.
As much as Premier Peterson's announcement is to be congratulated, it is the thousands of Save the Rouge Valley System organization volunteers to whom we owe our greatest appreciation. For over 17 years, SRVS has fought to protect the incredible wilderness as a park. The announcement is a tribute to their dedication and to their commitment.
We in this Chamber, and especially you, Mr. Speaker, can also be proud of the role that we have played in helping to save the Rouge. Over one year ago, the federal government committed $10 million toward the creation of the park in the valley and two months ago this Chamber unanimously endorsed a motion I put forward to save the valley.
Let us all celebrate this victory for the people of Scarborough and for the environmental future of Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance. Yesterday, the provinces rejected his efforts to get them to help him collect his goods and services tax. This means that if the tax should ever come into law, we will be the only country in the world with at least 10 different sales tax systems.
In his White Paper on sales tax reform in 1987, the minister said: "If all governments were to have different tax bases the system would be a national tax in name only. Effectively, it would be unworkable."
Yesterday, the minister admitted that if his proposal for a goods and services tax went into effect, he would be putting into effect a system which he himself said in 1987 would be unworkable.
Why is the minister trying to ram this tax through the House of Commons? Why does he not simply withdraw
it? Instead of trying to put through a tax he characterizes as unworkable why does he not go back to the drawing board and create a truly fair tax system for all Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, I believe that this will be a fair tax system for all Canadians. With the introduction of the goods and services tax credit, which will help low-income Canadians offset a good portion of sales tax, compared to the system existing today the new system will be much fairer.
The hon. member has referred to the fact that the provinces have not seen fit to join in with us to collect the tax. That is true. But there are a number of other efforts under way through which we are working with the provinces to develop ways of reducing the complexity of the tax to minimize the compliance burden. We are taking advice from the small business sector as to ways we can do this.
I believe that the result will be a less complex tax for the small business community and something which should provide a basis for expansion of that co-operative effort into the future so it will have more co-operation from the provinces and less overlap.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, small business people have a quite different view of the effects on them of the minister's goods and services tax.
John Bullock, President of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business said: "When you talk to a small businessman about operating two totally unharmonized retail sales tax systems you are talking about a nightmare." Those are not my words. They are those of Mr. Bullock, a leader of small business in this country.
Once again, why will the minister not withdraw this unworkable sales tax proposal, send his departmental officials back to the drawing board and tell them to develop a totally fair tax package for the country which would not be a nightmare for small business and which would be fair to all Canadians? Why will he not do that instead of trying to stick to a tax which he himself admitted, when he first started talking about it, would be unworkable if there was not one single sales tax base?

Mr. Speaker, for the last 50 years now we have had one royal commission after another, one task force after another. There have been five royal commissions, task forces and
March 28, 1990

committees recommending that we move away from the existing sales tax.
John Bullock agrees we should be moving away from the existing sales tax. The Canadian Chamber of Commerce agrees we should be moving away from the existing sales tax. The Business Council on National Issues, the manufacturers association, the construction association, the exporters and the importers have all recognized what the leader of the Liberal party has not recognized, that we have a tax system that, today, does not work. It is unfair. It is administratively so complex that the regulations for that tax are three feet long. It is time for us to change.
We have put forward a proposal which is quite workable. It is going to be a much better tax system for our exporters. It will put Canadian producers on a level playing field with the importers with which they compete.
Today, Canadian producers pay one-third more than the exporters with which they are competing. This is the change that we want to make and we believe it is a good change.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance said in his own paper two years ago, and I quote: "If all governments were to have different tax bases, the system would be a national tax in name only. Effectively, it would be unworkable".
I would therefore ask the Minister of Finance why he insists on imposing a tax on Canadians which he himself has said is unworkable and which small businesses see as a nightmare. Why do we need a tax system that is both unworkable and a nightmare?

Mr. Speaker, possibly it would be of interest to Canadians to know why the Liberal party wants to keep a tax that is deeply hidden in the price of everything that we buy. Possibly Canadians would like to know from the leader of the Liberal party why the party is in favour of a tax that adds a hidden tax to everything that we export. Possibly Canadians would like to know why the Liberal party is in favour of a tax that taxes Canadian products one-third more than the imports with which they compete.
Oral Questions
Would the Leader of the Opposition let us in on the secret? Why have they taken this stupid position?

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. He just finished quoting the Canadian Federation of Independent Business and the Chamber of Commerce as being supporters of his goods and services tax because they want to get rid of the present federal sales tax.
I want to ask the Minister of Finance if he is going to repeat that again because he knows full well that the Chamber of Commerce in Saint John last year and the Canadian Federation of Independent Business still today insist that if you cannot get this tax right by getting provincial co-operation you should stick with the federal sales tax because this is an administrative nightmare.
Is the minister denying that that is what the Chamber of Commerce and the Canadian Federation of Independent Business say?

Mr. Speaker, there are many organizations which agree that we should be getting rid of the existing sales tax. Even my hon. friend is on record as saying the existing sales tax is wrong and it should be changed. All members of the finance committee in the last Parliament-Liberal, New Democratic and Conservative- agree that the existing sales tax is a mess. We, as a government, have to take that advice. We, as a government, have to put up our proposal for the best way of fixing it.
Sure there are people who would like to have a lower rate. Sure there are people who would like to tax food. Sure there are people who would like to have a national sales tax, including the provinces.
We would like to have a national sales tax too but, unfortunately, the provinces are not ready for that. They know that there are things that they could do to help us improve their compliance burden and those provinces are helping us take steps to improve the compliance burden.

March 28, 1990
Oral Questions
The government has to move ahead. We were elected to govern. We were elected to face the problems of the nation. We are going to deal with one of the major problems that we are facing today.

I have a supplementary, Mr. Speaker. The Minister of Finance said earlier in answer to a question, that the new goods and services tax would be fairer than the present tax. Is the minister prepared to tell the House today whether his government will index credits for the neediest in this country? Will the credits for Canada's most vulnerable taxpayers be completely indexed? Yes or no?

Mr. Speaker, we are treating the goods and services tax credit in the same way as all other elements of the tax system. That is, it will be indexed at a level of consumer price index less 3 per cent. We have demonstrated time and again since we put in that provision that we make adjustments in an appropriate way to take into account the changing circumstances of people in low income brackets.
We have increased the refundable sales tax credit threshold from $15,000 to $16,000 to $18,000, and now, with the GST credit, it will be $25,000. We have increased the size of the child tax credit. We have also made changes in the income tax system that came into effect in 1988 which took 850,000 people off the tax rolls by making adjustments in the index formula.
That is precisely how this government will operate in the future. Where it is appropriate we will make the changes to improve the position of low income taxpayers.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Agriculture. As the minister is well aware, many Canadian farmers feel there is a crisis in this particular sector. Farmers deserve adequate compensation for all the work they do and for their production costs. This is only fair. Will the minister
immediately set up a national plan for farm income stabilization?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yes, I am indeed aware of the difficulties that the agriculture community faces, particularly in Saskatchewan and the prairie region where depressed prices, drought and other factors have led to a serious downfall in projected net farm income.
The hon. member asks whether we would put in place a new stabilization program. I can advise her that that is, indeed, one of the major priorities that is being undertaken as a result of the agriculture policy review.
We expect the task force that is studying this particular issue in depth to report back to us by April 30.
I might also indicate to the hon. member that I will be meeting with ministers of agriculture tomorrow to talk about the agriculture review process and options for the possibility of putting together a package that might alleviate the farm income situation as well.

My supplementary question, Mr. Speaker, is to the Minister of Agriculture. Of course the minister knows that the crisis is now. It has been going on, however, for some time. I would like to remind the minister that in October 1988 the Prime Minister said that we are not going to allow a single farmer to hang out to dry simply because the Americans and the Europeans have a subsidy war going on.
I would like to ask the minister about his program for farmers. It now appears that the United States is going to extend the American farm bill to 1995 providing American farmers, as he knows, with guaranteed protection against a depressed world market. Yet, here in Canada the government has failed to come to terms with this. Farm incomes here in Canada are expected to go down by 43 per cent.
We need those programs now. When will the government put Canadian farmers on an equal footing with American farmers and guarantee Canadian farmers the support equivalent to the price support that their American counterparts are going to have?

*
March 28, 1990

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, I am very much aware that the need is now and that is precisely why, in December, we set up a federal-provincial monitoring committee to look at the various facets of the farm income question. It is a multi-faceted question. The low commodity prices as a result of the trade war being conducted between the European Community and the United States is indeed a factor.
If the hon. member is suggesting that all the help farmers need is the equivalent of what the United States has been paying with respect to the Export Enhancement Program, I can tell her, for her information, that so far this year the Americans have spent $140 million on the Export Enhancement Program. I think the problem is much more serious than that and I can assure her that we will be dealing with it in that vein.

Mr. Speaker, I quite agree with the Minister of Agriculture that this requires a number of initiatives including the farm stabilization program and help to assist our farmers in getting a fair price for their produce.
I would like to ask the Minister of Finance about another initiative that this government could take. Canadian farmers are not suffering from inflation that the Minister of Finance so often speaks of; they are suffering from deflation. The minister knows that Canadian farmers are paying out billions of dollars in interest on land which is worth less than it was six years ago. This cannot continue.
Will the minister act immediately to look at implementing a program of protected interest rates for all farmers?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of the Farm Debt Review Board there is flexibility in the administration of that to take into consideration interest rate reductions and to take into consideration declining values in farm land. One of the areas we are looking at is an expansion of that program to make it more flexible in order to deal with the current situation, particularly as it applies in western Canada.
Oral Questions
I should say as well, for the benefit of the hon. member, that with respect to the livestock industry we just announced last week a continuation of the deferral program on the sale of livestock in the drought stricken areas of western Canada. If there are any other affected areas in Canada, we will apply it there as well.
I might ask the hon. leader of the New Democratic Party to prevail upon her colleagues when we do have important agriculture legislation like the crop insurance program, which was filibustered for two or three days by the NDP. That does not do a great service to the farmers or the people of Canada.

Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. The minister failed to keep his promise that he would not tax food. With the GST, the Minister of Finance is going to tax all baked goods. More than 85 per cent of Canadian families eat cookies, baked goods or pastry with their meals. Will the Minister of Finance finally admit to Canadians that he misled them, since he is also taxing food with his GST?

Mr. Speaker, this is a matter that is before the finance committee of the House of Commons. I think that is where it should be dealt with. Once the finance committee reports, then the government will respond.

Mr. Speaker, I hope the chairman of the finance committee is listening to the minister. Yesterday at a press conference, the president of Culinar stated that more than 300 jobs might be lost in East Montreal because of the GST. Will the Minister of Finance keep his word and refrain from

March 28, 1990

taxing food? Or even better, will he withdraw his proposed goods and services tax?

Mr. Speaker, the answer to the second question is the same as the answer to the first question.
The hon. member is talking about things that are currently being discussed by the finance committee of the House of Commons. Until it reports, it would be inappropriate for the government to make any comment.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Justice. I want to ask the minister a question that I raised with the former minister by letter and in the House of Commons in May 1988, namely the fact that Wilhelm Mohnke, a former SS officer, alleged to have murdered dozens of Canadian prisoners of war, is living today without challenge and in comfort in West Germany.
The minister, when I asked before, gave me an answer that was meant to imply some type of activity on his part. It now appears that he did absolutely nothing to press the West German government to act on this case. I want to ask the new minister whether she will take up this case. Will she press the West Germans, on behalf of the families of victims in Canada, to take action in the case of Wilhelm Mohnke?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like first to remind the hon. member that it was this government that did take up the question of war crimes and war criminals, instituted the Deschenes commission, and brought laws before this House which now make it possible for us to prosecute war criminals.
Unfortunately, the gentleman to whom he makes reference is a citizen of the Federal Republic of Germany whose own laws prohibit them from extraditing their own nationals.
We have as early as 1976 advised the West Germans of our information with respect to Mr. Mohnke, and there is an ongoing investigation. Unfortunately, under the terms of our international agreement with West Germany, I am not at liberty to reveal the details of that investigation except simply to say that it is ongoing and that appropriate efforts are being made to bring the information to the attention of the West Germans.
My officials have raised and discussed this case with the West Germans. I take the hon. member's question at face value as expressing his serious concern for this issue. I will certainly undertake to raise it in addition with my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs.

The minister pointed out the limitations of the government's present policies. These do not apply to German criminals because they are not prepared to extradite their own nationals. That is why it is important to make representations at the political level. The minister said she would make representations to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, but what is she going to do about the Germans, or what is her colleague going to do to ensure that something is done-in this case, about a war criminal living in Ottawa?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I cannot answer for my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I repeat what I said in English, namely that my department has been investigating the matter, and we are looking into this. As soon as I have anything to report to the House, I will do so.
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister.

Go on! Go on!
March 28, 1990

The Prime Minister has indicated publicly that he would not be scandalized, among other things, if Canada, the United States and Mexico had a free trade agreement.
Now that we are aware that the United States and Mexico are engaging in negotiations for a free trade agreement between those two countries, is the intention for Canada to be a participant in trilateral negotiations for a free trade agreement, or will there be an observer at the U.S.-Mexican discussions about free trade?
Mr. Speaker, in answer to the hon. member's question, I first want to say that his French was so impeccable it deserves the applause of all members in this House.
Hear, hear.

We are advised of the general interest of the Government of Mexico to expand its trading horizons with other countries, including perhaps the United States. We have received no formal notice of that, nor have we been advised of any arrangements that might directly or indirectly impact on trading arrangements that we have.
Should that come about, I can assure my hon. friend that we will exercise all the vigilance he would want us to in those circumstances.

I thank the Prime Minister.

I want to inform the House that your English is impeccable as well.
The Prime Minister has claimed that over 200,000 jobs have been created by the free trade agreement over the long haul of the agreement and that 25,000 of them were created last month.
I know the Prime Minister to be a man of his word. I have seen no evidence of those 200,000 jobs listed in detail or no evidence of 25,000 jobs created last month. In order to avoid the press criticizing the Prime Minister for not being accurate and backing up his statements, I

would ask the Prime Minister, through you Mr. Speaker, if he is prepared to table in detail those 200,000 jobs that have been created according to him by the free trade agreement and the 25,000 created last month, in French or in English.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans.

March 28, 1990
Oral Questions
Notwithstanding our current difficulties, the Atlantic fishery is a $1 billion industry that needs to be protected. Some are suggesting that aerial surveillance of our Atlantic waters will end with the elimination of the tracker fleet.
In view of these concerns, will the minister advise the House as to what measure he is taking to ensure that there is continuity of protection for this valuable resource?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that this question is prompted by a Liberal member raising this matter last week in order to have Atlantic Canadians believe that we are doing less. The fact of the matter is that there will be no lapse-and that was the suggestion-in air surveillance in Atlantic Canada.
If we look at this year, for example, we had something like 1,750 hours of air surveillance in Atlantic Canada. Under the new contract which is about to be announced at $28.5 million, this will go up to 3,850 hours. Even back home in Atlantic Canada that is more, not less.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister.

Yesterday, the Minister for International Trade confessed that he was not aware of the free trade talks between Mexico and the United States.
This is a government that prides itself on its veiy close and special relationship with the United States. Can the Prime Minister explain to this House how, when this trade deal has such profound implications for Canadian businesses and workers, his government was not made aware of it?

Mr. Speaker, I do not know why my hon. friend is offended by the idea of free trade, in view of the remarkable support free trade is now getting from the Government of Ontario. If it is good for Ontario, it has to be good for Mexico.
Oh, oh!

The Government of Mexico can initiate talks with whomever it wishes, at whatever time it chooses. It has not initiated any conversations of this kind with the Government of Canada, nor am I informed has it done so with the Government of the United States.
If there are exchanges which interest us or impact upon treaties that we have concluded, we will of course exercise that degree of vigilance that is appropriate and will intervene. I will be happy to report to my hon. friend as these matters develop.
On this point, Mr. Speaker-
Oh, oh!

-maybe I could quote for the Prime Minister an official from the office of the Minister for International Trade office. He said yesterday regarding the Mexican free trade deal: "One of the big advantages we were promised under free trade, preferential access to the U.S. market, could-disappear".
Did the government address these concerns when it was negotiating the free trade deal with the United States? If not, how could it have been so derelict in its responsibility toward Canadian businesses and Canadian workers?

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend will understand that I cannot comment on the views of an unidentified official who remains anonymous after my hon. friend's question.
The free trade agreement dealt specifically with the kind of concern that is being raised by my hon. friend. We put in the rules of origin provisions in the free trade agreement which prevent the kinds of things that my hon. friend is concerned about.
I noticed the other day that he said he was fearful of the fact that low wages in Mexico could have a deleterious effect on Canadian jobs. Make up your mind. If it's good for Ontario, surely it has to be good for other provinces and other countries.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having just returned from Africa, I wish to report to the House on my assessment of the current situation in Ethiopia, and recent humanitarian and diplomatic initiatives which Canada has taken in regard to the crisis in the northern part of the country.
Members of Parliament will be aware that some four to five million people in the northern Ethiopian regions
Routine Proceedings
of Eritrea, Tigray and Wollo are now seriously threatened by starvation.
I wish I could provide the House with assurance that serious loss of life could be avoided, but I fear that that is not the case. The situation created by the drought was serious, but it was manageable. When augmented by the ongoing military struggle in the region, the situation has rapidly deteriorated and is no longer manageable.
The tragedy is that not one single Ethiopian needed to die as the result of the current crop failure. Donor governments had responded generously and international and local agencies were poised to ensure delivery to those hardest hit.
A variety of channels were foreseen-distribution by the government within the areas controlled by it, crossborder operations supported by the NGOs from Sudan into the rebel-held areas of Eritrea and Tigray, and relief corridors crossing battle lines into vulnerable rebel-held areas of Eritrea, Tigray and Wollo that could not be reached through the cross-border operations.
This was a complicated package, but one that could have worked if two elements had been achieved. The first was the continued availability of the port of Massa-wa for the trans-shipment of emergency food aid supplies. The second was an agreement between government and rebel groups to allow the safe transport of food across battle lines.
The EPLF offensive of February, which saw the port of Massawa fall into rebel hands, and the continued unwillingness of the Government of Ethiopia to allow the port to be used for food shipments while still under EPLF control have effectively ended any chance of seeing through the present crisis without loss of life.
It is a sad fact that we cannot guarantee the delivery of essential life-sustaining food to the inflicted of the region, if the political entities that guide their destinies continue to use food as a weapon to attain their strategic military and political objectives.
That is not to say that we will not do all we can. We will continue to press for peace, and we will continue to use all channels available to us in an attempt to minimize the impact of this famine. I must, however reluctantly, conclude that we have passed the point of no return for many of those most affected, and it is only a matter of

March 28, 1990
Routine Proceedings
days until those agonizing reports of starving Ethiopians begin again to fill our newspapers and television screens.
Since the 1984 famine, which affected some 11 million people, our country has been one of the main providers of humanitarian aid in northern Ethiopia.
In all, the aid provided to civilians by the government and people of Canada has amounted to $300 million. This year, in addition to the approximately $26 million in aid that we have already sent through the United Nations and various non-governmental organizations, we announced initial commitments of $14 million for next year.
Canada has encouraged the warring parties to make peace and ensure the free movement of aid.
It has stepped up its diplomatic efforts: in Addis Ababa, we have had regular discussions with western donors, international humanitarian organizations and Ethiopian ministers and representatives; we have also contacted the Ethiopian charge d'affaires in Ottawa and held discussions with the Secretary General of the United Nations and officials of specialized UN institutions in New York, Geneva and Rome.
Finally, we have continued the dialogue with representatives of the armed opposition fronts in Eritrea and Tigray.
In all our consultations with members of the European Community, the Soviet Union, the United States, the Nordic countries and Ethiopia's neighbours, we have pleaded for humanitarian and diplomatic intervention.
On December 20, 1989, I appointed the senior vicepresident of CIDA, Douglas Lindores, special adviser on Ethiopia and its neighbours.
Mr. Lindores recently went to Ethiopia and the Sudan, heading a delegation of officers from External Affairs and CIDA.
The delegation met government representatives, representatives of rebel groups, of other bilateral donors, of the UN and non-governmental organizations, who are seeking ways to relieve the suffering of the Ethiopian people.
This week in Washington, Mr. Lindores met representatives of the EPLF and the TPLF, as well as a number of Americans involved in aid operations.
Just recently, Mr. Speaker, on March 18, the hon. member for Haldimand-Norfolk, the hon. member for Windsor-St. Clair, the hon. member for Kitchener- Waterloo and I had a meeting with President Mengistu and important members of his cabinet in the Ethiopian capital, a meeting that lasted over two hours. I explained Canada's position on issues of major concern including the famine, peace negotiations, political and economic reform in Ethiopia and human rights.
It is a fact that President Mengistu and his cabinet are under very strong pressure and have to manoeuver in the midst of a national crisis, but they do think the views of a country that has always provided assistance to Ethiopians are important.
During our meeting, I emphasized the need for immediately clearing a route to the interior of Tigray, in the south, and to use all other possible delivery routes to the north, including the port of Massawa.
I urged President Mengistu to deploy efforts for the resumption of peace negotiations between his government and the rebel forces.
I am referring to the negotiations conducted by former presidents Jimmy Carter and Julius Nyerere to bring the Ethiopian government and the EPLF closer together, and to those conducted by the Italian government with respect to the TPLF.
On March 20, the Ethiopian government announced that it would facilitate the relief operation which has started in the south, will cross the war zones and bring food to the north.
The Joint Relief Partnership, the JRP, consisting of the Ethiopian Red Cross Society and three church relief organizations: the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, the Catholic Church and the Mekane Iyesus Church, will channel relief to those who need it.
Perhaps, like me, you had the pleasure of watching television, last Thursday, when the first convoys arrived in the famine-stricken areas.

However, more-much more-needs to be done. The southern route must be supplemented by further intensive relief operations to ensure that food reaches all areas of the north. Traditional non-governmental assis-
March 28, 1990

tance to areas which can only be reached from Sudan must continue. I so informed the Ethiopian government.
As I have said, the port of Massawa is crucial if famine is to be avoided. To this end, it is essential that, notwithstanding the delicate political and sovereignty issues involved, the parties to the conflict take the high ground and make whatever arrangements are necessary to ensure the safe passage of food.
However, the determination of the Ethiopian government to recapture Massawa at all costs puts some shadow on that option.
I discussed these matters in Rome with Minister Lenoci of the Italian government and with the executive director of the World Food Program.
In Windhoek, Namibia, last week, I assured the United Nations Secretary General of Canada's support for an increased UN involvement in the relief efforts and the search for peace.
We should not underestimate the difficulties we face. On the one hand, rebel groups sense a final victory, while on the other, an embattled government struggles to preserve the territorial integrity of Ethiopia. Yet it is abundantly clear that only a just and enduring settlement of the Ethiopian conflict will bring to an end the suffering of the people of that country.
The peace process involving the Ethiopian government and the TPLF is resuming in Rome. The talks, under the chairmanship of Presidents Carter and Nyer-ere, are scheduled to resume in Nairobi, Kenya, April 8 to April 21, 1990.
The Canadian government has urged the Government of Ethiopia, the EPLF and the TPLF to accept that none will prevail by force of arms without unconscionable human suffering. We have urged them to pursue the negotiations to a successful and early conclusion and, in the interim, to permit the safe operation of relief efforts.
In this latter respect, belligerents are assuming a very grave moral responsibility.
Peoples everywhere have collected food to prevent famine and transported it to the region only to find that continued fighting is, in some key areas, interrupting
Routine Proceedings
delivery. How, in all conscience, can this be allowed? How can food deliveries be confined this way?
For my part, I am presently consulting with my colleagues from donor countries to underline the urgency of the situation and to ensure the greatest possible co-ordination in assuring food delivery to the needy.
At the same time, the Canadian government strongly supports an initiative by members of Parliament to mobilize international parliamentary support to seek an immediate agreement for the safe and assured delivery of all necessary famine relief assistance to all persons innocent to the conflict.
Let me end by reiterating the gravity of the situation as we found it.
Despite food aid which has been provided and will continue to be provided by the international donor community, fighting on the spot continues to hinder adequate, timely and sufficiently widespread delivery. A continuing stalemate in peace talks is unacceptable.
It is already too late for some. We appeal to the parties to accept that intransigency risks the lives of further innocent populations.
In conclusion, I assure members of this House, as we have assured the parties to the conflict and the chairmen of the peace processes, that Canada is ready to support the search for peace in any way that would be helpful.
I have received from the two opposition parties a resolution on the situation which we endorse. The resolution states:
That this House, noting that:
-	4 to 5 million innocent Ethiopians in northern regions of Eritrea, Tigray and Wollo, are seriously and unnecessarily threatened by starvation;
-	Canada is a major aid donor to the region today and was so during the 1984 famine crisis;
-and, further noting that Canada, with other western nations, could prevent today the loss of any life through starvation in the region;
-does unanimously condemn any and all parties to the conflict in Ethiopia, Eritrea and Tigray who would use food as a weapon to attain strategic military and political objectives, or,

March 28, 1990
Routine Proceedings
-who would not assist the international donor community to provide adequate, timely and sufficiently widespread delivery of food to the starving millions in the area.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, I would like to thank the hon. minister for reading my resolution and for having given her support to it. I also thank my colleagues on the other side of the House from the NDP.
It is with great sorrow and anger that we are reminded again today by the minister that some four million to five million Ethiopians living in the regions of Wollo, Eritrea and Tigray are once again on the verge of starvation.
We all remember so well the impressive and heartfelt response in 1984 of millions of Canadians from our poorest regions of the north to our wealthy businessmen of the south-those who responded so generously to the drought crisis in the same region which threatened 11 million persons.
It is with anger, a deep sense of outrage and even contempt that we realize that the current crisis is unnecessary but for the lack of political will on the part of all parties in the conflict between Ethiopia, Eritrea and Tigray. Government, rebel forces and parties outside the region encouraging the conflict must recognize and accept the condemnation of citizens and governments of the world who have tried in good faith to prevent the current impasse through diplomatic interventions.
I can only reiterate the words and sentiments of my hon. colleague across the floor that all parties to the conflict must take the high road, setting aside the political and sovereignty issues at stake and make the absolutely necessary arrangements to ensure safe passage of food to the innocent starving millions of Ethiopia.
Although we can all agree on this here in this House, I wish to impress upon the government that what has been done to date by the government and what we are doing here today is not enough. The minister has promised to continue to search for new ways to find a solution to lessen the holocaust which is beginning to take place again in the Horn of Africa. The unfortunate and
regrettable fact is that Canada has not continually mounted the pressure we have seen in recent months in order to avert this new disaster.
We have heard the government's financial commitment this year and the initial contribution for next year. But Canadians will want to know on an ongoing basis what other aggressive actions this government is taking to resolve the crisis.
We cannot allow cycles of misery to repeat themselves. NGOs, who have an extraordinary ability to provide aid in ways that are not available to governments, must be provided with all the resources necessary that they are able to absorb.
I would be interested to know what exactly is the support that the Canadian government is giving to the initiatives of members of Parliament to mobilize international parliamentary support to aid the victims. Certainly, there is a member on the government side well respected for his experience and expertise in the area by diplomats and the NGO community whose services it would seem to me should not be restrained.
All members of this House and the Canadian public will want to be kept informed of the government's initiatives with regard to this crisis. We do not want to sit back and watch a disaster unfold.
We and Canadian citizens want to respond-knowing that all possible measures are continually being taken by this government to stop the disaster-to prevent this from ever being repeated again.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to respond to the minister's statement on behalf of my party.
The tragedy of Ethiopia is not a partisan issue. It is a tragedy rooted in ancient quarrels and historic enmities complicated by the intricate interplay of competing national interests extending throughout the Middle East and the Horn of Africa. Compromise has not been a virtue among the combatants. Intransigence is a matter of principle even when it results in the slaughter of innocents. Hence, in this once noble land of riches beyond the needs of its inhabitants, a local drought is expanded once again by a general violence into an epic famine choreographing the ghastly scenes of thousands of children dying in the arms of mothers who can but wait to die in their turn.
March 28, 1990

As noted by the minister, all three Canadian political parties were represented in consultations in Addis Ababa with the representatives of NGOs, the Ethiopian government and President Mengistu. Our goal was to facilitate the delivery of food to the starving, to contribute to the negotiations for peace and to measure the significance of economic and political reform in Ethiopia.
Through the efforts of donor governments, international and domestic organizations, arrangements have been made to provide food if safe delivery could be assured. Canada alone has already committed $40 million to the effort. Horribly, the bellicosity of the combatants in the many-sided civil war limits that humanitarian intervention. Food is a weapon in this conflict and the deaths of thousands is now inevitable.
Much of the reason for this certain catastrophe is the capture of the port of Massawa by the EPLF and Mengistu's adamant refusal to permit the delivery of food through that port. The remaining paths of delivery are the cross border between Sudan in the north and the southern route for which clearance for the first convoy was given by the Ethiopian government shortly after our consultations at the Joint Relief Partnership.
An Ethiopian government proposal to employ a logistically difficult and costly airlift was pressed upon us but was not supported by the aid donors. Because of the failure of effective food delivery in the north, food will also have to be provided for refugees in the Sudan. The real solution to the crisis must address the real cause of this starvation-the war or wars that prevent the distribution of food.
That is why New Democrats support the minister in pressing President Mengistu to urgently pursue peace negotiations with the rebels, as we support the pursuit of peace to every other diplomatic channel available. In this regard we laud the efforts of the Italians and Messrs. Carter and Nyere at mediation.
We also support the proposal to initiate an extra-governmental effort by an international alliance of parliamentarians in support of the peace process.
Because of the nature of the conflict and the engagement of diverse interests, these will have to be neutralized, whether from the neighbouring Arab states, Israel
Routine Proceedings
or the major players of east and west. My party and I stand ready to support this effort to achieve the peace and, if necessary, to commit Canadian personnel and resources to keep the peace. Without peace, no effort, no matter how great, no matter how noble, can hope to save the millions who will die not because of drought but because of starvation wrought by enmity and war.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 PLIGHT OF WESTERN FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, very briefly, in my letter to you I outlined what I consider to be an urgent situation, that is the economic conditions facing western Canadian farmers. We know that they are the worst that have occurred since 1932, in the midst of the Great Depression.
The Farm Debt Review Board in western Canada recently reported that more than one-third of western farmers are in severe financial crisis. Bankruptcies and foreclosures are at alarming levels and predictions are that this year there will be a negative realized net farm income in the province of Saskatchewan. That means farmers will spend more money than they receive for the sale of their crops. They will have difficulty providing for their families and difficulty arranging the financing that is necessary to put in the coming year's crop.
Within the next three or four weeks, the farmers will be out attempting to put seed into the ground. As my letter also points out, the banks need three to four weeks to make a decision on an application for a loan. These loans are made on the basis of the cash flow of the farm. The bank wants to know how much money will be coming in and how much output there will be. They cannot make those calculations final until we and they, that is, the banks, farmers, and politicians know with some precision what sort of aid and assistance the federal government will be providing.
Since the two time limits are coming very close together, that is, the time limit for when seeding starts and when loans will be approved or rejected, it is extremely important that those announcements be made in the next day or so. Therefore, I move that in order to bring these matters to the attention of government, we have an emergency debate this evening.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-65 is a very important bill, and so far, this legislation has been debated for one hour and three minutes in the House of Commons. However, as all members will recall, earlier today, the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons gave notice that he would once again impose closure in other words, limit debate on this very important question.
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of Bill C-65 is to authorize the government to borrow up to $25.5 billion, which is 25 thousand million dollars. Canadians know perfectly well that when such enormous amounts are borrowed for the coming fiscal year, 1990-91, which runs from April 1, 1990 to March 31, 1991, that these amounts are needed to cover the government's budget deficit.
As we know, in his 1990 Budget the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) announced that he intended to go to the financial markets to get this $25.5 billion.
Government Orders

Mr. Speaker, as you can see the government will borrow an amount which is less than its projected $28.5 billion budget deficit. This is because non-budgetaiy transactions will generate another $7.5 billion of revenue, which reduces the amount the government needs to borrow from financial markets.
These non-budgetaiy transactions include government employees' pensions accounts-this is the public service superannuation account which has a healthy sum in it which the government regularly borrows every year. It means they can also use accounts payable, cash in transit, and outstanding cheques. So that $7.1 billion is actually government bookkeeping, which allows them to use moneys they do not actually own but which they use to reduce or pay off the budgetary deficit by such transactions.
The $25.5 billion borrowing authority requested in Bill C-65 is accounted for as follows. The government deficit is $28.5 billion, the non-budgetary transactions are $7.5 billion; reducing the amount of $28.5 billion by $7.5 billion leaves $21 billion; exchange funds earnings will bring in about $1.5 billion, the foreign exchange contingency fund will bring in an additional $3 billion, for a total borrowing authority requested of $25.5 billion.
Members can find a complete explanation of the borrowing authority requested in Bill C-65 on pages 109 to 110 of the 1990 budget.
While I am on my feet, I would like to remind you, Mr. Speaker, that I am sharing our allotted 20 minute time with one of my colleagues.

Mr. Speaker, considering that Bill C-65 accompanies the Budget and seeks authority for the government to borrow to cover its budget deficit, I would strongly advise anyone with a desire to understand these transactions to consult the so-called post-budget analysis, a veiy impressive document prepared by experts in the field.
Mr. Speaker, now that I have basically explained the purpose of the bill, I am prepared to yield the floor to any members who may wish to comment further on this legislation.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Questions or comments? Resuming debate. The hon. member for Welland-St. Catharines-Thorold.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to take up where my colleague left off on the borrowing bill C-65.
The sum of $25.5 billion is one which boggles the imagination. The salaries of thousands of Canadians would still not add up to the money this government is borrowing at this time to carry out programs which, for the most part, are programs that have been cut back from their election promises.
As the borrowing bill itself deals simply in money matters, I would like to put a face on this particular borrowing bill. In addition to the moneys which are going to be raised, ironically to carry out programs which are cut back, the House should also look more particularly at other revenues that the Minister of Finance is raising.
Last August, the Minister of Finance released details of his goods and services tax. After the presentation, he told reporters that nobody likes this tax. Then he added: "Let me be quite clear, we are absolutely committed to going ahead with this tax". He also announced that the goods and services tax, the GST, would create billions of dollars a year in revenue, would increase exports and create jobs. If this tax is supposed to create so many more billions in revenue, what in the name of goodness are we doing borrowing an extra $25.5 billion?
One of the questions which comes to mind is, if nobody likes this tax, why go ahead with it? Second, why indicate that this proposal will be implemented regardless of the feelings of Canadians, irrespective of any debates or committee hearings? Witness the charade that has been going on for the last few weeks in the finance committee. We have had filibusters. We have had the chairman of the committee, if not making a fool of himself, sometimes making a fool of the committee itself. I do not think that this is in keeping with our parliamentary procedures.
I and many other members of Parliament have tabled petitions. I have tabled over 14,000 names on petitions against this GST. This has all been done in the last few months. These signatures represent the opinions of thousands and thousands of Canadians. This is in addition to the letters addressed directly to the Prime
Minister, the Minister of Finance and other elected members of Parliament.
We have a right to wonder if the government is listening to the people of Canada when it collects all of these billions in taxes. My colleagues say that it is not, and I agree with them absolutely. If it was listening to the people of Canada, then surely it would withdraw this terrible tax which is heaped upon the backs of those people who can least afford it.
The statement "absolutely committed" which the Minister of Finance made, is a clear signal to me that the government intends to impose this extra burden on Canadians, who have already contributed $120 billion to the treasury in 1989. That is $50 billion more than when this government took office in 1984. But it will not even listen to the plaintive and angry voices of Canadians who are so adamantly opposed to the goods and services tax.
On December 9, 1989, the Minister of Finance put forward his 7 per cent solution, stating that he had listened to Canadians. He must have listened to every Canadian I did not listen to because we have not been getting the same signals. The people of Canada have clearly stated that they do not want the GST and the new 7 per cent package is no more fair than the 9 per cent package was.
The issue is not whether we generate enough money to look after ourselves, but whether the government has the ability to plan and govern. This very day in the House, we are asked once again to give the government carte blanche to borrow $25.5 billion and we are supposed to do so with a glad heart. I, for one, am not at all enthused about granting them this extra money to play with, so that they can do what? Spend it on their big business friends and cut the programs of the poor? No, the government will not be getting my support on this.
I referred to the $50 billion more which the government collects in taxes every year than they did in 1984. The extra $50 billion, which was collected through a myriad of taxes, could have taken care of the deficit. Remember, this was a government that was elected on the basis that it was going to cut the deficit. It has doubled it in the five years that it has been in office.
There would have been some money left over to start retiring our big national debt. Here again, we have seen increases of staggering proportions. In 1983-84 the national debt was $160 billion. Projections for the end of
March 28, 1990

the fiscal year 1989-90 show our national debt reaching $351.6 billion. What a fantastic amount.

Even with these $50 billion, the deficit which was $32 billion in 1984 is still $30 billion per year more than we collect in taxes, and this is a government that claimed it knew how to cut spending in government operations and throughout the country. That has not been the case, Mr. Speaker, and I am looking forward to 1992!

Canadians are informed that family allowances will be cut because the government has no money. Senior citizens must face an uncertain future confronted with decreased old age benefits and this damnable clawback that the government has put forward.
This decrease is commonly known throughout Canada as the "clawback". I wonder why they did not just call it something gentle. Can you imagine the spectre of a great big claw coming down upon you? It is like the American eagle coming down on the little mouse and that mouse, in his last act of defiance, sticking out his tongue at the great American eagle. The Canadian people cannot stick out their tongues except to gasp in horror at how the government has mismanaged the affairs of Canada.
This is nothing more than a broken promise, or a set of broken promises. It is a frightening change in social policy, a change which is being implemented without prior consultation with the seniors. The clawback will soon be followed by another devastating tax, the infamous GST, the goods and services tax. Seniors and other Canadians agree that the deficit must be reduced. I agree with that. They also know that the goods and services taxes introduced in other countries have gone up 20 per cent.
My learned colleague on the other side takes this as a jest, as a joke that should be perpetrated on the Canadian people. I wonder if the people can pick up his laughter from across the aisle, as they are struggling to make ends meet in their homes with this extra burden of taxes. I would advise my hon. colleague, with all respect, that his laughter should not take place in this House. This laughter, if it is laughter at all, should be hidden
Government Orders
away from the ears of the hardworking Canadian people who must pay these taxes.
We have made valuable suggestions to the government so that all Canadians might share the burden fairly. Did it listen? Not at all. It was far too busy preparing a costly advertising campaign which was misleading and in contempt of Parliament, as was said by the Speaker himself, and finally had to be abandoned because, to put it mildly, it was slightly premature if not illegal.
The GST will add to the cost of most essential goods purchased by ordinary Canadians. The Canadian Home Builders' Association says that the GST will increase the price of a typical new home nationally by $3,000, which is more than six times the cost estimated in the technical paper prepared by the finance department. Is this just more misleading of the House and of the people of Canada?
Cuts in housing rebates for low income Canadians amount to $400 million. The proposed changes to the GST do not address the affordability problem or housing for low income Canadians. In other words, the government is not listening.
This government is not doing anything to alleviate the burden it places upon Canadians. The increase in the cost of housing will vary by market areas from a high of $9,200 in Toronto and $4,700 in Vancouver to $800 and $1,000 in Charlottetown and Tlrois-Rivieres respectively.
Some services have been designated as tax exempt. This does not mean the end result is tax free. For instance, a day care centre that is tax exempt will not charge the GST on its final invoice for day care services to parents. The day care facility will have to pay 7 per cent or more on all its purchases of books, equipment, et cetera. It will have to raise its fees to parents to recover these added costs.
Mr. Speaker, I see you are signalling me that my time is running out. I have many more points I would like to make, but I would like to end with these last two.
The list of taxable goods and services will now include such things as haircuts, funerals, stamps, taxi rides, cheque books, lottery tickets, car repairs, and a host of other items which Canadians buy every day. The Minister of Finance has exempted brokerage fees, underwriting fees and foreign currency trading, all items purchased predominantly by upper income Canadians

March 28, 1990
Government Orders
who could more easily afford to pay the new tax than average Canadians.
My last point, Mr. Speaker, and I have many more that I would like to make, but as the critic for youth for the Liberal party, I have said many times in the House that the future of Canada lies in the well-being of our youth. I have said we must educate them, train them, and give them a sense of responsibility in being a Canadian.
What kind of government is it that puts taxes on books, pens and on the very things so necessary to acquire an education in order to take their place in society? No, I am not in favour of this borrowing bill. I condemn the goods and services tax which I believe will be seen as one of the most dastardly bills ever put forward in the House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, I listened very carefully to my hon. friend. He reminded us that the legislation asks for the borrowing authority for $25.5 billion. That seems like an awful lot of money to borrow. I worry about borrowing $5,000 or $6,000 to buy a car. I start thinking about the payments and so on. But we are being asked by the government to give it authority to borrow $25.5 billion. I cannot even imagine what that would look like if it were in a pile. All I know is it is an awful lot of money.
I cannot remember when the House was asked to do something like this, to give authority to the government to borrow $25 billion. At the same time the government is saying it does not want to talk about it. The government has just given notice to stop debate.
I want to ask my hon. friend, a parliamentarian of long standing who has been here a long time and knows how things have gone over the years, if he can recall any time in the past when the government has asked to borrow so much money. The government is running things so badly that it is desperate to impose this 7 per cent goods and services tax. Can the hon. member recall any time when the government has asked to borrow so much money, but at the same time does not want to debate this legislation, so it will invoke closure to muzzle the duly elected
people of Canada and keep them from responding to this request? Can he recall any such request in the past?

Mr. Speaker, not only can I not recall sums of this magnitude being asked for in the House of Commons from the governments of which I was proud to be a part, but when we tried to borrow sums of $5 billion to $7 billion it was viewed as the most enormous sums that had ever been asked for by the Government of Canada.
My colleague asks a question and to let him know that not only are they borrowing this money, but according to a study by the Canadian Council on Social Development and the government's own sales tax documents, a middle class family with two children and a total income of $45,000-$27,000 from one parent and $18,000 from the other-will have their taxes increased by over $3,400 in 1991, $2,797 by previous Conservative tax increases, and by $629 for the GST. We are asked to permit this GST to go through and to grant the government this enormous sum. This is truly unheard of in Canada.
I for one would associate myself with any members who would oppose this borrowing bill. The government must be brought to its senses. The best way to do that is right here in the House of Commons by pointing out to it the mistakes made and the mistakes it is making. Hopefully, this government will not make them in the future.
Mr. Speaker, this is the first time I have spoken in the House before closure was invoked. I really do appreciate that.
They have given us notice though.
It's like having a crystal ball.
I wish to speak against the borrowing bill. We recognize that the government requires money to run this country, albeit very poorly. We object to the priorities of the government.

speechtext: Could I ask the hon. member if he will speak for 20 minutes, or 10 minutes plus 5 minutes?

Hopefully, about 20, Mr. Speaker.
During my 20 minutes I will refer to a couple of my favourite books. One is entitled Tommy Douglas Speaks.
