March 28, 1990

That is a non-fiction book. The other one is Where I Stand by the right hon. Prime Minister and that is obviously a fiction book. Any resemblance between these two gentlemen will be purely coincidental.
When you hear the quotes from both books it is hard to differentiate between the two in what they say, but certainly in what they did and do are very, very different.
Mr. Douglas often said that fools, charlatans and evil doers will be exposed in open debate, with present company of course exempt. He also said: "We won't give up the fight against the government despite the adversity, despite their jackboot tactics, their non-democratic closure, their GST". He did not say some of this but I am paraphrasing it. That is exactly what he meant when he said "We are going to-" and I best not get too far astray from what Mr. Douglas said. "If your cause is just and right sooner or later you will win. It must triumph because it is a part of the warp and woof of the universe. No matter how many setbacks there may be along the road, you may be sure that someday the right and just will prevail. It will prevail simply because it is right and just."
That is why, despite the fact that this government tries to muzzle the opposition and the Canadian people from speaking against its policies, we must continue in the House and outside of the House to fight the government and its heinous policies.
This borrowing cannot be taken out of context of the budget. It is part and parcel of it. Everyone knows that the New Democrats stand for total tax reform, that this kind of willy-nilly borrowing and this kind of budget process would not be necessary.
My hon. colleague from Nickel Belt has become somewhat infamous, as far as the government is concerned, with his corporate bum of the week announcements. I asked him to provide the names of some of the groups of whom he has spoken these past several weeks. I am sure he will have another 20 years to go because there are so many.
I was disbelieving when I was told there were 86,000 profitable corporations in the country which did not pay tax. I did not believe it. In fact, it has proven to be 90,000. I will cite just a few cases. Perhaps the names are best unstated. With profits of $214 million one received a tax credit of $2.12 million. Another with $75 million profit
Government Orders
received a tax credit of $2.86 million. But in its heart of hearts it found some money to donate to the party in power. I suppose that is honourable.
Revenue Canada answered when asked to define a large corporation that it is a corporation that makes about $7 million. My next question was why would a special tax of $.0175 be put on corporations that had profits of $10 million? The answer was to be fair and give or take a couple of million, what is the difference? One has to wonder if at the poverty level if a couple of thousand would not make a difference to the poor in this country.
Mr. Douglas said "the art of governing is the art of foreseeing, having a crystal ball". I agree with that. The Prime Minister from his crystal ball said in 1983: "It is a continuous fight card in which it is difficult to find winners and easy to identify the loser, Canada itself". It seems the phrase "the common good" has been struck from our vocabulary. The Prime Minister was prophetic as well but sadly prophetic. The common good seems to have left the country. Policies breed cynicism in the country. He has lost not only his foresight but lost his physical sight.
It is very easy to trace the losers in this budget. As a result we have to go through this borrowing bill. The losers are the prairie farmers, maritime fishermen, natives across the country, women's centres and the provinces. The have provinces have to suffer a little more than others. In that have group is the province of Ontario which is well off compared with some of the maritime provinces. Some people forget-in fact, the government has totally forgotten-that northern Ontario is part of the have province of Ontario.
We are not doing all that well and the government is not going to assist us, certainly not through the budget. Its acts of deregulation, privatization, reprofiling, rationalizing and all the buzz words of the government are not going to do anything for us. They are going to hit us in a very heavy-handed, negative fashion.
That brings me to my most unfavourite topic. All this is part of the government agenda. The free trade agreement was supposed to bring us all wealth and save each family $800 per year as the Prime Minister said. That is not happening. It was supposed to create 250,000 jobs. This past Monday I attended a forum in Sault Ste. Marie, Michigan. The Canadian official in charge of implementing the deal said that the free trade plan has been a bit player in the over-all picture. He also

Government Orders
admitted that it has failed to secure access for Canadians into the United States market. He has admitted that.
Gordon Ritchie, the former free trade negotiator, really is a candid individual. He said just this past week that free trade will not be a major creator of jobs. It will not be. That was a "specious claim". That means something that appears to be the right thing to say but, in reality, it is not true. It was a specious claim made in the heat of an election campaign. The Prime Minister made that specious claim 20 months before the election when he told Canadians free trade could produce hundreds of thousands of new jobs.
It seems that what they said and what is happening are both, indeed, specious claims. It is just not working out to our benefit. I have cited this so very often and I have had the opportunity to meet with our American counterparts. I found out what they thought about free trade. Their words to us are: "Don't bite the hand that feeds you. Canadians, keep quiet. You are not going to get any more of our market. Please realize this. Don't rock the boat". When our own negotiators and the American politicians tell us the same thing, I suspect we have some problems.
The indication was that social programs would not be hurt and, in fact, they would be enhanced. Well, unemployment insurance is not being enhanced. Family allowances and old age security certainly have not been enhanced. The government has attacked universality, even though it would not admit it. All of this is part and parcel of the government agenda-the government policy-that we react so negatively to. Therefore, we must vote against this borrowing bill for all of the wrong reasons.
I want to come back to the GST. I was going to bring a backdrop of probably 15,000 cards from bowlers, dance teachers, skating teachers, music teachers, small businesses, veterinarians, and everybody. You name the group. They are all hostile to the GST. If the government is going to plough through with it, and it gives every indication that that is what it is going to do, it is going to realize a cash cow with multi billions of dollars against the desires of any Canadian. It would appear that the government is against the will of the people, at least 80
per cent of them and probably it is growing on a daily basis.
Yet the government says there are no tax increases. We know full well that that is not true. The tax increases will be passed on to the provinces and the provinces in turn will pass them on to the municipalities and thus we see some of this negative reaction by municipalities, including my own. That is one reason that they are hostile toward government in general. Some of the actions may not be the message that wants to be delivered, but it is a message of desperation: Is anybody listening out there to a lonely voice in the wilderness up in northern Ontario?
I think all would agree with Mr. Douglas' philosophy and our party's polity that humanity comes first. We believe the measure of any community is the amount of social and economic security which it provides to even its humblest citizens. I do not know anybody in the country who would disagree that we do stand for that. The Prime Minister suggested that he also agrees. He said: "Then there is what I call the dimensions of tenderness. It is that vital responsibility of government to demonstrate a compassion for the needy, an assistance for the disadvantaged, the equalization of opportunity for all and an elevated sense of social responsibility that must continue to find favour with every thoughtful Canadian". We agree with the Prime Minister. Mr. Douglas agreed with the Prime Minister, but actions speak so much louder than words. The government's policy does not in fact exemplify what the Prime Minister said in 1983 and I suspect people would agree with that as well.
How did this budget come about? I will not cite exactly the words, but I will paraphrase the Prime Minister when he said that budgets must come as a result of a great deal of public consultation. It must be a consensus of the Canadian people before a budget is brought forward. The people must agree with the direction of the country. We could not agree more. We think it is a great idea.
Well, we know how the budget was struck last year-in the dead of the night. We know how it was struck this year. The Minister of Finance said he was too busy to meet with people this year. He was too busy. There was no consultation. He sent out 50 letters. I asked to whom he sent those letters and was told: "Well, we can't really tell you to whom we sent the letters." That is an
March 28, 1990

interesting point unto itself. I did not pursue it. Maybe it is not important. I do not know, but it certainly does not give any indication of consultation or consensus.
I want to talk about positives. Canadians look to leadership to display some innovation, some creativity, and some positives. I have been here for 16 months and all I ever hear are negatives from the government. It is the old "We have to cut VIA Rail to make it better" and "We have to cut your social programs to make them better". In the budget, I read the list and it is a litany of cuts. There are no positives. That is why the Canadian people say we despair. There is nothing positive for us anywhere.
I would like to touch on a few local issues that really hit home, a microcosm of the big picture, if you will. VIA Rail is selling off its excess stock-selling it off. We have a tourist attraction in my community that will have to spend $25 million to $35 million to buy new cars or to refurbish old cars. It is the single major, most significant tourist attraction in our community. The government could say that perhaps this community or that community, or maybe this enterprise, could use this excess rolling stock, and maybe it could sell it to them at a bargain price. What a lift it would be to the community. But no, the decision of Transport Canada thus far is to privatize the sale of it. Contract it out, give it to a consulting group or a marketing agency, and it will sell it back to you. The cry was that we have been subsidizing VIA Rail for half a billion dollars every year. Now the government is going to do us a big favour and sell excess rolling stock to us at market value. What an excellent opportunity that could be seized to make a lot of people happy-and probably save the municipal and provincial governments some money down the road.
I have a humorous example. That is the FBDB and its now infamous funding of 38 strip clubs across the country to the tune of $17 million. I can understand why the government is a little bit skittish about continuing that kind of process because Canadian taxpayers were kind of aghast at that. I am sure the government members were as surprised as we were and somewhat aghast that Canadian tax dollars went to that kind of entertainment.

Some of them weren't.
Government Orders

Some of them weren't. Okay, some of them knew, right.
Anyway, it has reacted to that now and it is saying that it has got to be very, very, very cautious, not only with FBDB but also FEDNOR funds.
There was an application in my community for a renovation to a tourist motel/hotel, if you will. Last year, it had one piece of entertainment that might be considered off-colour by some people, but there was every indication that FBDB and FEDNOR would be giving funds to this group to complete its renovation. Because of the new policies and the new restrictions, it is conceivable that funding could get cut off. I can understand that, the fearfulness of spending money on those kinds of enterprises. But, can a person be persecuted because he had one show last year, and would give an undertaking that he would never ever again present that kind of entertainment in his establishment? That was not enough. He gave that undertaking.
The next thing was to get from the Member of Parliament, myself, a letter stating that I did not think this establishment would destroy the moral tone of my community. I went ahead and gave them my okay on that. One has to wonder if there is going to be porno-police. It is also going to measure the gallonage of beer out of that establishment. It is a classic. I do not know if this is to save money, to save face, or whatever.
Another example is the Sault Locks which is a landmark in my community. It is 100 years old. Books have been written about it by the Canadian government. The present government says: "We want to walk away from it. We want to give you $5 million. Privatize it. We do not want any more to do with it." That will tear the face off my community unless private investment comes in to assist the government. I hope that does not happen, because the Americans-they have told me this-will want us to participate in the financing of their super-lock to the tune of $250 million, just across the river. But our government says: "We will wait and see what happens." We are going to save money now, but we will have to spend millions in the future, because the Americans will insist that we do so.
To conclude, Mr. Douglas said the only freedom which the NDP would destroy is the freedom of the few to

March 28, 1990
Government Orders
exploit the many. The only people who need fear us are those who are seeking to live by the sweat of someone else's brow. Our agenda never changes, and it shall not, because it is right and just. The good will out in the end. We will be voting against this bill because of the government's abusive policies to the Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, first, I would like to compliment my friend on his presentation to the House today.
I would particularly like to ask him to turn his attention to what has become an institution in Canada in cultural methods and also in communication, the CBC. I am speaking in particular of one of the areas in the west in British Columbia. I know that many of my constituents in Okanagan-Similkameen-Merritt listen daily to Canadian Broadcasting Corporation radio and also watch CBC television. There were the cut-backs of, I believe, $140 million in 1989, and the cut-backs of some $20 million in this particular budget. Many of the people in my constituency and many of the people I have spoken to in contacts across Canada are somewhat concerned in that what is being attacked here is not simply another radio station or another Crown corporation. What in fact is being attacked in the cutting of funds to CBC radio and television is our cultural communications system across Canada.
They listed all of the programs that they listen to. One of the things is the thread that goes across Canada in the phone-in programs on Sunday mornings. I know that my young daughter, who is only 11 years old, listens to a number of programs on CBC radio which she finds not only entertaining, but also educational. I have had letters from people in small communities such as Midway, Greenwood, Bridesville, Osoyoos and Christina Lake, asking us to point out to the government that these are their links to the rest of Canada, and part of what they consider their cultural heritage. I wonder whether those from northern Ontario feel the same way about CBC and these cuts. Would he have any comments on the fears of the people in my riding and in fact in all of British Columbia?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his question. This once again ties into the whole issue of the Canadian fabric in our society. Cuts in the CBC are just another attack on the Canadian fabric as we know it. Yes, the CBC is looked upon not only by Canadians but by people around the world as being special, as being an excellent broadcasting operation.
People are now looking more and more south rather than east-west, not only in communications but unfortunately in trade and sometimes in cultural and recreational pursuits. It is part of a much larger scheme.
If I might hit very close to home and refer to the House of Commons, the CBC will be forging an agreement with a private cable company for House of Commons coverage. I think just about everyone endorses the loosening of rules in this House, but in a minority report my party expressed some concerns that the CBC is forming a partnership with a private enterprise. That is another blow to the CBC.

I have a short question, Mr. Speaker. I listened with interest to my hon. friend's comments. I must say I found them to be most interesting and very educational. He went on at some length about a number of initiatives that the government has failed to take. I think of things like not funding the forest sector adequately, cutting back on regional development grants, cutting back on support for the small business sector, and not providing much endorsement and support for tourism.
I asked myself what good the government has done. We can think of all sorts of things it has not done that it should have done and we can all think of all kinds of things that it has done that it should not have done, such as the imposition of the goods and services tax.
I was racking my brain, as I was listening to my hon. friend, trying to think what this government is noted for accomplishing that people would perceive to be positive or useful.
Can my hon. friend think of anything that this government ought to be recognized for, other than a host of very negative initiatives which amount to the dismantling of the infrastructure of Canada?
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his question. I too, even as he asked the question, was racking my brain to come up with something positive.

The winds of dissent are there. To answer the hon. member's question, I cannot think of anything. The only thing positive, perhaps, is the fact it has have achieved 17 per cent in the polls and I think Canadians think that is very positive. Let us hope that that positive wind across the country will continue.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate on Bill C-65, the borrowing authority bill. As many of my colleagues before me have said, we are dealing with a request for authority for the Government of Canada to borrow some $25.5 billion.
Traditionally it is an opportunity for members to comment on how the government makes use of the tax dollars of the people of Canada and how it goes about collecting those dollars. It is an opportunity for all of us to comment on a wide variety of programs and policy.
I came today prepared and armed with a long list of specific grievances of my region and indeed the country in general with respect to the fiscal policy of this government. I decided, instead, to put aside that list and to talk in more global terms, global in the Canadian sense, about the policies of this government and where those policies are leading this country.
We have a new theology at work in Canada today, a different kind of approach to government and one which on the fiscal side, I humbly submit, contributes as much to the great frustration and division in the country today as do questions of constitution in particular.
In other words, there is a lot of anger and frustration in Canada today. There is a sense by many groups, regions and individuals within society that they have been abandoned by the national institution, by the national government. Out of that grows a sense of frustration and that frustration is personified by lashing out: sometimes lashing out at neighbours; sometimes picking on minority groups; sometimes, unable to get at
Government Orders
the source of your frustration, reaching out and attacking those nearest you.
That in a nutshell personifies the mood of this country today. Why is that? I submit that that in large part is happening because the kind of contract we as Canadians have had with each other from sea to sea, across ten provinces, across two language groups and through the multiplicity of our multicultural institutions, which has always bound us together as a nation has been dissolving over the last period of time.
It used to be that if you lived in Newfoundland you knew that you could aspire to equality of opportunity. You never expected to be equal in every way with every other province, most notably the wealthier provinces. You did not expect the same quality of highways necessarily, or even the same quality of municipal services, or even as many or as bountiful green spaces and park lands, but you did expect equality of opportunity. You had a belief, if you lived in Newfoundland or lived in Aqaluit or in Chimo, Quebec, that at least you had equality of opportunity. While your personal or community circumstances could not be said to be equal to the most prosperous parts of the nation, at least your opportunity or your chance to succeed as an individual in your society was there. That meant that in fundamental areas, no matter where we live in Canada, no matter what our circumstance or language, the notion of citizenship, the notion of being a Canadian meant that we were equal in fundamental ways.
What are the ingredients of ensuring if not equality of circumstance at least equality of opportunity? Surely the first and foremost among those ingredients must be the right to a good education, access to quality institutions, the ability to train the mind to acquire the skills to compete in an increasingly competitive world. Is that not the first and foremost ingredient necessary to participate in the notion that there is equality of opportunity? Traditionally in this country it has been. I believe that traditionally Canadians believe they have had equality of access to good education.
What is another ingredient? It is very basic: access to health care, good health care, quality health care. No matter where you lived, no matter what your personal circumstance, when the need arose to have access to good quality health care, whether you lived in Quebec, British Columbia or Newfoundland, you had equal access. Traditionally that has been the case in this

March 28, 1990
Government Orders
country. It is another of the fundamental agreements that is part of the contract called Canada, one of the things that binds us together no matter where we live as being a fundamental component of the notion of Canadian citizenship.
There is another part of the contract that has kept Canada united, and that is the notion that even though we acknowledge that there are disparities within the nation between regions, and even within provinces between regions, between those who have and those who do not on the economic side, the Government of Canada would always intervene to try to reduce the gap between the have and have not parts of this country. That has been another primary tenet of the notion of citizenship in this country.
I submit that the fiscal policy of this government that is now asking to borrow $25.5 billion in Bill C-65 has dissolved the basic Canadian contract. Why? When you cut billions of dollars as this government has in its last budget-in fact in EPF alone $7.5 billion in health and education out of transfer payments to the provinces-y-ou set up a system where the notion of equality of opportunity is destroyed. Even though the cut to Ontario over five years is $1.2 billion and to Newfoundland is only $164 million, the reality is that Ontario is more able to make up that shortfall, if that is the decision of the Government of Ontario, and maintain the quality of both health and education programs in Ontario than is Newfoundland able to make up a $164 million cut in the province of Newfoundland.
So what happens? Some provinces of Canada have the fiscal ability to maintain, if it is the determination and political will of that jurisdiction to do so, the quality and standards now available in health and education and other provinces, even if they have the will, have reached the limit of their borrowing capability. They cannot borrow any more and they cannot tax any more. A province like Newfoundland where the sales tax is already 12 per cent has only one option left, and that is to raise user fees for either health care or education or to eliminate programs.
That is what is happening. Those provinces that do not have the fiscal capability are being forced to eliminate
programs. The fundamental notion that as a Canadian I have fundamentally equal access of opportunity is gone and in certain regions of this country, as a consequence, there is an acknowledgement of that cold brutal reality, a fundamental sense of frustration at the loss of what Canadian citizenship used to mean. There is a fundamental sense of rejection by the national government for those kinds of regions; not only Newfoundland but many other provinces as well.
That kind of feeling brews frustration, a frustrated nation unable to reach out the thousands of miles to strike a blow, even metaphorically. The government that has authored this policy begins to reach out and strike a blow at neighbours. It is that kind of policy that contributes to the lack of tolerance which exists in Canada today.
Since 1969 regional development has been institutionalized in this country, initially under the auspices of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, the sole purpose of which was to combat regional disparities, reduce the gap between developed and less developed regions and, although not to guarantee equality, at least to provide the possibility of development, the basic infrastructure to allow industry to develop in regions where it currently is not the case.
That has been the basic philosophy. We can sit here and argue in this House about whether or not it has been successful. We can talk about whether or not dollars spent in the combat against regional disparity have always been well spent and whether we always got the best bang for our buck, but if we believe in the concept of this federation we cannot dispute that combating regional disparities is a fundamental obligation of a national government and has been a fundamental characteristic of modem day Canada.
That policy has been abandoned by this national government. We have seen a dramatic cut in regional development expenditure in Canada, an abandonment of the notion of investment in infrastructure. We essentially have a polity that says to those who want a different quality of life than is now available to them: "If you want a different quality of life, man the wagon trains and resettle".
March 28, 1990

It is a national resettlement policy. Whether it is the
65,000	people who have been pushed off the farms in Saskatchewan, run off the land in the last four years, or whether it is the thousands of fishermen who have been run off the water in Atlantic Canada over the last couple of years, we are seeing in this country, not by accident but by design, an abandonment of our primary producers and those who live in a rural lifestyle, those whose wealth is primary wealth.
There is not a member of this House who generates one cent of wealth for Canada. We operate on the fringes, on the froth of the economy. We are part of the great service sector. We are elected to be here representing our constituents, but we do not generate one cent of wealth. Those men or women who go out and put their hands into the land and yield from that land a crop that feeds this nation and the world are primary producers. That is real wealth being generated for Canada. The fisherman who goes out and harvests the sea, the humble fisherman, the gentleman who barely subsists on an income below the minimum wage, generates far more wealth for Canada than any member of this place because none of us generate a cent.
Yet the policy of this government that wants another $25.5 billion-an incredible figure-has been to abandon those primary producers. These people are frustrated. They are angry. They want to be here. They want to look across at the Prime Minister who is abandoning them, the Prime Minister who said: "You can trust me". They want to have their say, but they cannot because they cannot reach across the thousands of miles of the great land that is Canada and have their say.
So, in frustration, they reach out too often to those who are closest, their neighbours, and there is more intolerance in this country. It is not bom out of an intrinsic intolerance in Canada, but out of frustration.
When we hear, as we do these days, all of the talk and discussion about Meech Lake, constitutions, potential amendments, resolutions and solutions, I ask myself whether it is not time we understood that a large part of the poison injected into the bloodstream of Canada did not find its way there yesterday or the day before or the week before, but found its way there as a consequence of the policy of a national government in fiscal terms which
Government Orders
has melted away the glue that has bound this country together over the decades.
The fabric of Canada is not the flag beside you, Mr. Speaker. It is but a symbol, albeit an important one. It is not the Parliament Buildings. They are but a symbol, albeit another important one. It is not even the border between Canada and the United States, which is another important symbol. The fabric of Canada is to be found in the hearts, the minds and the souls of Canadians.
Unless you can go to Quebec and find in Quebec people who believe that every bit of Canada from Cape St. George in Newfoundland to Prince Rupert in British Columbia belongs to them, then you have no fabric called Canada. Unless you can go to Newfoundland and find there Newfoundlanders, Canadians who understand that the problems they confront daily in their lives are the same problems being confronted by the average family in Quebec, then you have no Canada.
Until we understand and until this government understands that the policies, the contract, the commitment we gave to each other as Canadians by way of equality of opportunity in fundamental areas, the commitment to combat regional disparity and indeed in simple terms, to share the wealth and opportunity of this country, are fundamental tenets of this nation not to be melted away or dissipated as a consequence of the bottom line necessity of meeting the budget projections of the Minister of Finance, I submit that all the other ongoing negotiations today about how to bring peace to this country will continue to miss the point.
As a member of this place who has been here for 10 years, I am increasingly convinced that this Prime Minister shall preside over without radical intervention the Balkanization of this great country, the dismemberment of this great country. Until there is some awareness on the other side that high stakes poker is no game to be played with the future of a nation, I cannot support Bill C-65. I cannot support this government's request to borrow another $25.5 billion. I cannot support continued administration by a political party which has not only cut deep into the Canadian psyche, which has not only begun to dismantle it, but has cut through the meat, the fat, and into the bone and has drained the marrow of the wellspring of goodwill that once was Canada.

March 28, 1990
Government Orders
I call upon my colleagues in all parts of this House and from every region of Canada to reject Bill C-65, not to grant the current Government of Canada another $25.5 billion in borrowing authority, and to be here to ensure that when the time comes this motion is rejected. Hopefully this government in Canada's interest, because it is a money bill, will put itself and this country out of our collective misery by quickly going to the polls because time is running out.

Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the member for the usual passion and emotion with which he gives his speeches. I suspect that some of that may come from his staff member who hails from Sault Ste. Marie, who has good Italian blood, and was a student of mine some 25 years ago. I will not give her all the credit.
Nevertheless, what the member said is certainly what I would want to say about this country. There is much doom and gloom among Canadians and parliamentarians. I am sure that even some of those members across the way are somewhat desperate in their feelings about what is happening to all of the regions in Canada.
Is there any hope for us, I ask the member very seriously. What will transpire in the next year or two years or three years? Do we have hope for the country? Does he have hope for the country?

Mr. Speaker, I have the greatest hope for this country. I have a profound belief in the gut desire of Canadians to build and unite this country, to keep it growing and prosperous. I am not naive about the fact that this country is in difficulty. The country is not in difficulty because on March 28 we do not have an agreement on the Constitution. The country is not in difficulty only because on March 28 we have a continuing process, a difficult and frustrating one, on the Constitution. We did not get to where we are today because we woke up yesterday with a problem called the Constitution.
I am saying to my friend and to all members of the House, and through the House to Canadians that I believe a considerable amount, a lion's share of the origins of the increasing intolerance we are experiencing in Canada today on matters that have to do at least on the surface level with the Constitution, can be found in the fiscal policy of the national government.
I do not separate fiscal policy from social policy or from regional development policy. If you take away all of the national institutions, if you take away from the country those things that have been part of the contract we have made with each other for 100 years, then you dissolve as well in the minds of Canadians no matter where they live, and in particular those who live farthest away from the centre, their attachment and commitment to the federation.
The fundamental glue that holds a country together is not a constitution. That is profoundly and unquestionably important. Fundamentally what holds a country together and develops a country is ultimately what is in the hearts, souls and minds of Canadians.
Increasingly as the days, weeks and months go by there is little and little more daily, weekly and monthly left of our national institutions with this government. Any and all of the destruction of the CBC, the elimination and destruction of regional development programs, the abandonment of health and education programs, and a transfer of the debt to some of the poorest provinces and jurisdictions in this country contribute to division in the country because they take away the national institutions to which we attach ourselves in the communities in which all Canadians. Intangible examples of the value and the wonder of being a Canadian are eliminated. You treat the nation as nothing more than so many bits on the Monopoly board. If that is the bottom line, if that is the way we ask Canadians to measure the value of their Canadian citizenship, then we have sold our soul and sold our heart for the bottom line.
That may make the Minister of Finance very happy. That may motivate him when he wakes up in the morning. That may get his juices flowing, but it does nothing for the ordinary Canadian and it does nothing for the people who today want nothing more than for this country to succeed.
This fiscal policy, this request for $25.5 billion more, is pathetic in the face of the problems that we have, and it would be pathetic for Parliament to grant these moneys to a government that has not understood the root cause of the difficulties we confront in Canada today.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member mentioned the CBC, and I mentioned it in a prior question to my friend from Sault Ste. Marie. Would he like to comment on the
March 28, 1990

thread of what I and others have seen in the budgets of this particular government over the years?
It has attacked of the thread of national unity, whether it be through privatization of various Crown corporations, cutting funding and perhaps ultimately privatizing institutions like the CBC, whether it is the cut-backs on VIA Rail and the elimination of the Silver Bullet.
In this particular budget, the government proposes the ultimate sale of PetroCan, something which was brought in by the member's own government with some approval by my party, a corporation that is now becoming somewhat profitable and well run. Now that it has become profitable, and there is an opportunity of getting some money back into the coffers, it appears the government wants to get rid of it.
If the government negotiates as well as it did in the sale of de Havilland to Boeing, it is going to end up costing us money. Would the member like to comment on the destruction of the Canadian cultural and ethnic fabric that is set out not only in this budget but in previous budgets of this government?

Mr. Speaker, my hon. colleague who has just spoken has given us a thorough list of those institutions. We can make the analogy that those institutions are arteries in the body that is Canada and they are being severed. The country is not exploding, it is imploding. If all the arteries are severed, the heart ceases to function. That is what this Prime Minister has never understood.
A fisherman, in a community on the great northern peninsula, said to me one time: "If that fellow Mulroney was a lake, you could walk across him and not even get your ankles wet. He has no depth". I thought that was a profound insight: no depth, no vision and no understanding that the kind of magic that is required of leadership is not to be found in the flow charts, not to be gleaned from the words of wisdom of the pollsters, pundits, the Dalton Camps, the PCOs and the PMOs. The kind of wisdom necessary to appeal to what is fundamentally good, tolerant and positive in Canadians is better to be found in the heart of that fisherman than to be found in the
Government Orders
cold graphs offered in the polling data that the Prime Minister spends too many long, lonely hours with.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1990-91 MEASURE TO ENACT

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Wilson (Etobicoke Centre) that Bill C-65, an act to provide borrowing authority, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1990-91 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill before the House is the borrowing bill in which the government is requesting authority to borrow some $25.5 billion.
When considering this request, I think we have to ask if the government has the ability to manage, as it say it has. It has been pointed out by the hon. member from Kamloops and other members, that if this is management, this country is in for a rough ride. The type of management we have seen since the election of 1988, is management by time allocation and closure. The government with its arrogance and authority, has seen fit to manage by cutting off free debate in the House of Commons and to ignore totally the wishes of the Canadian people.
We witnessed again today the House leader of the government party advising us that he is going to close off debate, essentially before debate is started. After only

March 28, 1990
Government Orders
one hour and three minutes of debate so far, we already have notice from the government that it will not allow any more debate on this borrowing bill for $25.5 billion.
This is in addition to the government's ridiculous attitude toward debate. Last week we were debating the crop insurance bill, a bill that both the Liberals and the New Democratic Party decided should go through and be passed in the best interests of Canadian farmers.
Before asking for any input, the House leader of the government party simply said: "Bang. Closure. No more debate." We ended up voting on the closure motion on a bill that neither the Liberals nor the New Democrats had opposition to in principle, even though they believed that perhaps it should be expanded as suggested by some amendments that had been proposed.
We have now experienced closure 13 times in the last year and three months, and time allocation another 10 or 12 times. It is getting to the point where I wonder what it is this government is managing. It is managing to cut off the freedom of expression and the freedom of debate of the people of Canada.
That is not what we are here for. That is not what the Canadian people have voted 295 members of Parliament into the House of Commons for. They have elected us to review, read, study and to debate in their interests the bills before Parliament. That process has been cut off, constantly and totally by this government in its arrogant use of those jackboot tactics to slash the debate already on this major borrowing bill before anybody has had the opportunity of speaking on it.
I shake my head, along with the people of Canada. This is how the government is managing change. The change it is managing is the change in the democratic process of allowing reasonable debate on all legislation that comes before the House.
If there is an apology to be made to the people of Canada, it is the apology that we have to use what methods are available to us in opposition to combat the arrogance of a government that is willing to use these Draconian methods, these measures that were brought in to be used only as a last resort. We are now seeing these methods being used as the primary resort. Every bill, regardless of what it is, if it looks like it is going to be debated, is met with closure. No more debate. We can
talk on it today and that is it. Nobody else can speak on it.
That is what we have seen in the committees going across Canada, whether it be the unemployment insurance or the finance committee. The government sets up a schedule that we must follow. If not, you are cut off. It does not matter whether you are a member of the House of Commons or whether you are a public citizen. While you may want to be heard, if you do not fit within what the government sees as the area it wants to hear or you do not fit within the time frame of the government's schedule, then you cannot be heard. Is that democracy?
When we see what is happening in eastern Europe, with the democratisation of the eastern European countries and the Eastern Bloc countries, and we look at what is happening here, I scratch my head in amazement and wonder: Are they progressing and are we regressing? What is happening to us?
I would like discuss now what I have seen happening since I have been in Parliament, specifically dealing with the borrowing authority and the budget.
Last Thursday I attended a forum on literacy. This is the International Year of Literacy. In the city of Penticton I saw a play which showed the difficulties in Canada of literacy. I did some reading to see what was available for Canadians.
Approximately $110 million has been provided over a five-year period for the promotion and study of literacy, although the demand is much greater and immediate to fund existing programs and to start up new ones to combat the actual problem. The need now is for core funding for literacy projects and for education of those who are illiterate.
Are you aware that there is somewhere between 4.5 million and 5 million people in Canada today who are functionally illiterate, Mr. Speaker? In my province alone, there are 360,000 people who are functionally illiterate. In looking at the studies that have been done across Canada, unfortunately it shows that as we go further to the east, the illiteracy rates rise.
Being functionally illiterate does not necessarily mean that those people cannot read the spoken word. It means that they cannot function because they cannot put enough words together in many cases to be able to understand the everyday forms that they have to fill out for income tax or for their child tax credits or, as the
March 28, 1990

GST comes through, for their rebates on the goods and services tax. These are the types of skills that they need.
We who can read take it for granted, as those of us who can see and those of us who can hear take those senses for granted. We do not see how serious this is. In fact, if you take our sight and our hearing away from us, it is not much different than taking away our ability to read. It is a mode of communication that is essential for many people.
The play that I saw really hit home. It is called Reading the Signs. It is a play by a Canadian playwright, Jim Betz and produced by World Literacy Canada and performed by the Young People's Theatres. I would strongly suggest that people get out and see this play if it comes to their area.
I implore the government members to go to see this play because it shows what I talk about when people ask where would I spend money and where would I save if I were in government. It is a matter of priority. It has been shown, time and again, that if we teach those who do not know how to read and write to be able to do so, they become more employable. They become higher income earners. I think the figures show us that those who are literate earn 44 per cent more than those who are unable to read and write. This is what we should be addressing when we are trying to make a better Canada.
I implore this government to see this play, Reading the Signs, because it is an excellent play showing the difficulties of those who cannot read and write and the problems that they go through in everyday life, the problems that those of us who can read and write, who are functionally literate, do not even recognize.
In many cases we do not even recognize when we see people making excuses about why they should not read a particular document or letter. But this does puts us on our guard, and makes us more aware of some of the things that are so important to many of us out there. I implore this government to look at that. The $110 million is a good start, but perhaps somewhat misdirected.
In looking at future budgets and in looking at this budget, I ask the government to consider putting more money toward training teachers, more money toward the
Government Orders
programs and the core funding required to look after the problem of literacy in Canada.
Let me move on to one of the things in the budget that was particularly upsetting to me as seniors critic for my party, namely, the cuts concerning veterans. This has hit home in an area that I represent, Okanagan-Similka-meen-Merritt, where we have a fairly high seniors population, almost triple the national average, many of whom are veterans.
The Royal Canadian Legion from Grand Forks wrote to me on March 7 and I would like to read this short letter into the record because I think it is relevant. It is from Branch 59 and it reads as follows:
Branch 59 of the Royal Canadian Legion, Grand Forks, British Columbia would like to express our very deep concern about the cuts to veterans allowance in the government's budget of April, 1990.
Surely the veterans who were identified in the Veterans Improvement Program are, as they get older, more in need than ever.
Particularly shocking was the decrease in subsidization of the costs of veterans in intermediate and long-term care facilities. Virtually doubling the veterans portion of these charges from $240 to $400 per month is a cruel blow to those ageing and dying veterans who so willing jeopardized their well-being in the service of Canada. Many have not long to live, and to make savings on their hardships seems particularly insensitive.
It will not be long before the numbers of all veterans will be seriously depleted and eventually disappear, but in the meantime, it is the intention of this branch and hopefully the entire Legion membership to rise and defend their comrades who are least able to defend themselves.
It is a shame that our government's memories are so short.
To balance a budget on the backs of the least fortunate of our society is a public disgrace.
It is signed by the president, Rae Hayward.
I could not have described better than Mr. Hayward in this letter the disdain and disgust that I feel in the cuts to the allowances and the programs that are there to protect and assist those who have fought in both wars and in the Korean War so that I can stand up freely and speak my mind in the House of Commons. I am very pleased to have been able to read this letter into the record.
Equally as shocking, at a time when we pay pay lip service to women's issues and the equality of women, is to have the government attack by cutting core funding to women's centres on top of a 15 per cent last year, of $2 million, I believe, to a cut of some $1.3 million this year. Again, it is a disgrace. It is not only an attack on women, it is attack on all Canadians. Those women's centres

March 28, 1990
Government Orders
offer so much. The women's centre in Penticton in my area will shut down as a result of this core funding cut. They will try to continue it on a volunteer basis. L. Burnham of that centre has been a hard working member of the Penticton and area community.
This group has done such things as spearheading a drive for family housing, investigating the need for day care. They have sponsored workshops on such important subjects as poverty awareness and family violence. They have provided a library on subjects of interests to women. They have been sending out regular newsletters to keep concerned people aware of the local and national issues and they have run a series of leadership development workshops for women.
They also participate actively in the women's shelter and the assistance with the women's shelter that is so key not only to Penticton but to all of the small communities around Penticton such as Osoyoos, Oliver, Okanagan Falls, Cawstin, Summerland. All of these areas are drawn in and looked after by that particular shelter in the city of Penticton.
I am not the only one who worries about these cuts to the women's centres. I received a petition which unfortunately is not in a form that would be presentable in the House but I think the message of the 87 people who signed this particular petition is relevant. They protest the federal budget cuts to women centres and transition houses throughout Canada. The services provided, especially those involving emergency shelter and safety, are essential to the welfare of women, their children and pivotal in the struggle to end family violence.
I speak of these cuts I return to the question of priorities. If we are to come out of the dark ages then we must take steps toward the equality of men and women. It is a small thing when you consider the little bit of money that is required in order to fund core funding for these women's centres or even to expand them.
When we consider that this government has seen fit to proceed with a program of advertising of over $14 million for the goods and service tax when it knows that over 80 per cent of the people of Canada do not want, that in
itself is a comment on the priorities of this government. Do not give the people what they want but what you want and then proceed to sell that program to them with their money. What Canadians need is more things like women's centres and arms of our communities that will help those who are less fortunate.
Finally, I would like to comment on the environment. When I read the budget and listened to the minister's budget speech I wrote down in the margin "Lip service but where is the money"? That is exactly what has happened.
There appears to be no money for the environment. There are cuts to just about everything else. There are cuts, it appears, in the Forest Resource Development Area, an area that would assist in silviculture and reforestation of our forests at a time when, particularly in British Columbia, we recognize how important our forests are to us for the future.
The government has not set anything aside for that and it is talking about substantially less money being available. The FRDA agreements come up for renewal at the end of this month, a short few days away. We fear that if those programs are cut it will be costly not just in jobs but to the environment.
What is not in the budget with respect to the environment is the funding for conservation and alternative energy programs as promised in the last election campaign. Funding for research and development and environmental technologies as promised in the Throne Speech is not in this budget. There is, however, the cap on much needed overseas aid and development. There are no new funds for reforestation programs. There are no attempts to deal with global warming or disintegration of the ozone layer. There are no cost sharing programs for conservation, recycling and mass transit programs.
There are also all of the cuts in VIA Rail, an area that perhaps we should be looking at to ensure that those of us who are so ready to use our cars for transportation might turn to if we had a rail system that is more efficient and more effective and ran more often. But what happens is a constant attack on these systems.
March 28, 1990

I wind up as I started. The government says it will manage change. Well, Mr. Speaker, if these are the changes that we are managing to get then I think it is time that we managed to change this government.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to congratulate my colleague on a fine speech and congratulate those who have preceded him this afternoon.
It seems strange that when there is a bill to borrow approximately $28.5 billion that we would hear absolutely not a peep, not a squeak, no justification coming from the other side of the House whatsoever.
Is this a sign or is this an extension of the malaise that has set in in this country, that the government would suggest to Canadians who are watching that it does not have to justify this borrowing? Are the members saying they know where they are going and they can assume that is right.
Canadians to whom I am talking are not assuming it is right, I can assure you of that. I just wonder if I could get some reaction from my colleague on the fact that there seems to be nothing, no justification whatsoever coming from the other side of the House to argue, at least present a case to the Canadian people to suggest that they know where they are going or what they are trying to do with this nation.

Mr. Speaker, certainly from what I have seen in the short time that I have been in this House and as a student of politics and Canadian history for most of my life, I think the hon. member is correct. We have a government that simply proceeds with what it wants as opposed to what the people of Canada want. It promised one thing in the election, as I have explained with the environment, but it has come through with something totally different, nothing.
In the last Parliament the Tories said nothing at all, and in fact were against the free trade agreement. They turned around and before the end of Parliament, we had a free trade agreement on the table. It is an arrogance that I have seen building, particularly over the last few years with this government that, the majority's will must be the will of the people, regardless of what the thoughts of the people are. I think the attitude of the government here is a small snapshot of everything we have seen over the last little while, the clawback on the old age security
Government Orders
and family allowances. People did not want that but they are getting it anyway.
There is the goods and services tax; 80 per cent of the people in Canada are against it but our Prime Minister knows best and we are getting it regardless. We are getting it without the ability to debate or change it. The Tories are doing it, what they feel is best for Canada.
The unemployment insurance changes hurt not only my province but many of the other provinces across Canada. Again, labour did not want it, many management people did not want it, and certainly the municipalities are going to end up paying a lot of extra dollars as a result of being employers. It is shifting the balance of payments from one to the other, from one pocket to the other with the taxpayer ultimately being the loser. It is all done by essentially a thumbing of the nose at what in fact Canadians want. The government is simply saying, "There is what is on the plate, you children of Canada, eat it and be happy and do not give us any back talk".

Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief. I think the member has brought to the debate a slightly different perspective, one to which we probably do not give enough priority. It is the concept of people who are literate, but not functionally literate.
I am sure that he experiences this in his office, as I do in my office, and as do members of our staffs to a greater extent. It concerns the forms that average Canadians are expected to fill out. I refer to forms from Revenue Canada, Canada pension appeals or immigration and disability credit forms. Any kind of application that comes from this government must be a tremendous burden to people just trying to get through them. Those of us who are fortunate enough to have extensive education have a great difficulty ourselves.
I would be very interested in the hon. member's comments on the complexity of the forms, something which seem to go against the people who are already disadvantaged.

Mr. Speaker, something that we in Parliament have to work toward is the simplification of forms, not just forms for income tax but simplification of all forms. We should put those forms in plain words, English or French, so that the people can understand them. We do not need the wherefores and the heretofors

March 28, 1990
Government Orders
that we so often get in the legal jargon. All that does is confuse people.
What we should be striving for is what we are now seeing in the insurance and legal areas where there is encouragement to get rid of the old-fashioned language and getting down to basic, easy English and French so that we, the average person out there, can understand. We should not need a Toronto lawyer to interpret these things. We want to be able to interpret them ourselves without the necessity of some high-falutin accountant or lawyer having to be employed to do it for us.
In that vein, I would like to bring up two things that I have not touched on. It is an expansion of what we have heard here today. I refer to the cuts in citizenship and multiculturalism and the cuts in native funding.
In each of those areas, if we look at English as a second language, and in some of the areas of citizenship and multiculturalism, built in to them is part of an educational process that I mentioned when I was speaking of the illiteracy problems within Canada. Certainly, the cuts to the native programming have been a knife thrust to the very heart of a problem that we have here in Canada.
If we look at the Southam News study on illiteracy, we see that it looked at Canada as a whole, but did not go into the territories where we have a high native population. What the study showed was that often, because of the lack of training and opportunity, those in our native communities do not have the opportunities that others do to gain an education. Therefore they are not able to take advantage of some of the government programs because they do not understand the paperwork. They cannot fill out the paperwork because they do not even know it exists.
I am saying to the government, shake your head and refocus on what is important to keeping this country together. Let us get on with the job of managing Canada in a manner that keeps it intertwined and happy.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1990-91 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this debate, which has been going on for some time now, brings to everyone's attention the importance of the financial crisis being faced by this government. Although it is fond of talking about market forces, about what the opposition did when it was in government and
about what the provincial governments are doing, in reality it has put Canadians into a comer, something which we all feel very badly about and which we wish we were not in.
The bill in front of us, Bill C-65, authorizes the government to borrow $25.5 billion. I would like to take time to show ways in which that affects people in Winnipeg North Centre. I think the people in that constituency deserve an explanation because as taxpayers they are carrying the burden. That is because there has been a tremendous shift in our Canadian tax system away from the corporations and on to average families. In fact, we see that most of the people who are hurt by this deficit are those who can least afford it.
It is hard to interpret these policies for people who do not follow the government closely every day and who do not have to watch it in Question Period, as we do, trying to defend policies which are indefensible. It is hard to understand why it caused this financial panic in the country. I call it a financial panic on purpose.
Before I arrived in the House of Commons two years ago I spent my time teaching political science at the University of Winnipeg. The question that is very basic to political science is the question that is asked by one generation of scholars after another and that is: "Who gets what, where, when and how?" It is also a question that journalists ask.
A country gets itself in trouble when it loses its sense of legitimacy, when it loses the will to be taxed and when it loses the sense that what their government is doing is correct. It is then that people begin to revolt. When Canadians look around and ask themselves that basic question of who gets what, where, when and how, they begin to feel that this country is spending money contrary to the democratic principles on which the country was founded.
We chose to build this country and to tax ourselves out of a sense of purpose, whether that purpose be defined on a regional basis; helping people in the north build communities, helping people in the west establish farms, helping people in northern Ontario establish mining and lumber communities, helping maintain the fishing industry in the maritimes, helping Toronto to grow into a
March 28, 1990	COMMONS DEBATES	9903
world class city with financial strength or helping Vancouver develop as a port. There was a decision made that we would help each other. At times the west has been a great generator of income for this country; and at other times the west has had to turn to the central government and say: "Please give us a hand". Similarly, we could go across each of the regions in this country and point to times in which they needed somebody's help.
When we become as bankrupt as we are now-and the government can use any figure it wants, but we are probably dealing with a deficit of $35 billion and rising each day-people realize that we can no longer help each other. When we say that we can no longer help each other, then the very fibre of the country is at risk. When we have to deal with a bill such as the one in front of us today, we have to come to grips with the fact that government has put the fibre of the country at risk because we cannot finance our efforts to help each other out.
We have at other times listened to the government and to members of all parties talk with a great deal of seriousness about the constitutional crisis facing us. It is wrapped around deadlines, factions, what one provincial government wants to do versus another and what opposing leaders want to do. For all these reasons there is a great deal of tension in this country, but nobody sits back and thinks of the relationship between the economics of Canada and the constitutional crisis.
I use this opportunity to say that there is a direct link. People are less supportive of our country right now because they do not feel they have a stake in it. All they have is a bill. If you want to be like Ronald Reagan and argue in family homilies, then the reality is that people feel less committed if they cannot continue to work together and produce an income; if they cannot continue to look after their own homes and if they cannot look after those who are sick. People become depressed. This country has become clouded by a depression which was caused in part by a government strategy which has raised taxes among those who are least able to pay for it and who are struggling the most. That strategy does not turn and give out money to the poorest people in this country in the poorest regions who desperately need it. In fact it pulls the money out of the system and creates more and more debt.
Government Orders
The government made the strategic decision in 1984 that it had to lower taxes on the rich and increase the taxes on the poor. It is a variation of the American thesis that the rich do not work because they do not make enough money, and the poor do not work because they make too much money. The government decided what it would try to do was give the rich more money and at the same time take the money away from low-income Canadians.
That strategy has created incredible tensions in the country, whether we define rich by region or by families, or whether we define the poor by certain groups in remote parts of Canada or in our cities, whether we are talking about the homeless, children, or native families on reserves across northern Manitoba. The poor are not getting anything back. So when we look at a borrowing bill we say: "Who are they borrowing it for? What has happened to our tax base in this country?" The strategic decision to lessen the tax burden on some people in the hope that they would generate so much income and that money would be replaced has absolutely failed.
The second strategy that is now becoming apparent and is failing is the free trade agreement. I know people will say right away: "What has free trade to do with taxation? You are off the mark, Mr. Member." It has a lot to do with taxation.
The federal government has made the decision to reduce all sorts of revenue bases dealing with international trade. When people talk about reducing tariffs and subsidies, it means that the government is losing an income base. The GST argument is based upon not only the inefficiency of the manufacturers' sales tax, something which nobody would deny, but as free trade takes effect, the government loses a large revenue base. The logic of a North American marketplace, governed by market forces and not by government action, and not by government leadership, is that you lose your taxation base in that economy. This is what is happening to Canadians right now. Canadians are afraid.
I am thinking particularly of the city of Winnipeg. It is a great city and has played a great role in this country. But the reality is that right now Winnipeg is under a tremendous amount of pressure. People in that city feel it with their hearts and are looking for a way of redeveloping it. There are many groups that have been formed and so forth. They turn to the federal government and say: "You have been a partner with us. You have helped form Winnipeg. You helped, for example,

March 28, 1990
Government Orders
with the CN which goes through the city. You helped with Air Canada. You helped with a number of government institutions. You helped build up our hospitals. You helped transfer money to our province. We are there and now we are ready to do something".
The federal government turns on the government of Manitoba and the people of Manitoba with a vengeance and says: "I am sorry. Do you not see our deficit? Do you not see we have no money for farmers or for western economic diversification? Do you not see that we have to move CN out to Edmonton or back to Montreal? Do you not see that we have to close down VIA and pull Air Canada out and privatize it?" The list is endless. The end product of that is that a total depression sets upon leaders in a city and a province who are trying to rebuild and to grasp a role for it.
Winnipeg threatens to become a city of wholesaling and not a city of manufacturing. That is not because it does not have the ambition, but because the reality is that the government is doing absolutely nothing to help it out. I hold this federal government and these ministers responsible.
If you looked through the articles in the newspapers after the budget, a time when people raised some very serious complaints about this government and the budget, what did you see? We saw that the Minister of Energy said: "Manitoba gets so much money they should not be complaining". Can you imagine that, Mr. Speaker? This is a city which has been impoverished through federal government inaction for the last five years, and it has to apologize for asking for money. What kind of country do we have when we have to apologize for asking for money when there is a legitimate desire to grow, expand and be a healthy city?
The fact that the government has consistently tried to make the people of Manitoba feel guilty about asking for money was one of the most sudden turnabouts in government policy, particularly in a party which has spent years deciying federal intervention. When it was asked what it was going to do for the city of Winnipeg, it said: "Sorry, we have no ideas. We have no money. We hope you do well. We are going back to Ottawa. We have
cabinet meetings. We have this and that to do. We are not here for you. Best of luck".
When people go back to that basic question of who gets what, where, when and how, they find out that in the case of Manitoba, Winnipeg and the constituency of Winnipeg North Centre, it is not them. They do not know how other people do it. They know it goes elsewhere. They know that the large sums are being lost in carrying out activities which are not beneficial.
The purpose of any member's response to a budget is not to decry on behalf of one region, but to use one region as an example of the tensions being created across this country. I am sure members who sit on this side, whether they are from Kingston or Ottawa, share in my anguish and frustration that the government chooses to hurt so many parties through this budget.
I would like to spend some time talking about the fact that this is one of the few times in Canadian history that Canadians are literally refusing to pay taxes. Those of us in the west who read the accounts of public meetings being held in Winnipeg, in Estevan, Regina, Saskatoon, Calgary, Edmonton know that on the prairies people are saying: "We will not pay the tax. We do not want the GST."
People realize that we have a huge deficit. After the war we had a huge deficit. People did not refuse to pay taxes. We introduced income tax in the first world war to finance the war. Yet here we have a crisis and people are walking on us. As politicians we have to ask these questions. Why are people walking on us? Why are people not willing to finance government? It is because of the irresponsible action of the people sitting across from me that people refuse to pay their taxes now?
The question for the Minister of Justice and the Deputy Prime Minister who are from the west, and the Prime Minister who never comes to the west is this. "How far are you going to push Canadians?" Is there, among you, a Maggie Thatcher who thinks that people can be policed into paying taxes? Are we going to have the same sight in Canada that we do right now in Great Britain of people in fist fights and people being bullied into paying an unfair tax?
Canadian leaders, particularly those across the aisle from me, have to learn that they cannot push people into a situation like that. Canadians are trying, in their usual gentle fashion, to say they do not want to pay this tax. It is not because we are irresponsible. We simply want you
March 28, 1990

to get your house in order. Until the government gets its house in order, people are going to continue to reject and to fight that tax. I think that they should be supported because the tax is inherently unfair. The borrowing of money to do things which are contrary to the interests of average Canadians is unfair. Generally speaking, when everyone sees an unfairness, then I think you have to turn around and say: "Let's stop and let's listen."
In England, Maggie Thatcher made the decision that she did not have to listen, that she was above listening, that she was above democracy. Right now she is paying the price for that. She is having to deal with people in the streets being hurt by their fellow citizens. What kind of country do you have when people turn on each other rather than pay taxes? You have the beginning of a national crisis.
The last thing that we need in Canada, given the national crisis we are already in, is a tax revolt. It is incumbent upon each and every minister of the government, to review departmental budgets and find ways of reducing expenditures, cutting out waste and, more important, to speak to the Minister of Finance and tell him: "Get those interest rates down. Speak to the Bank of Canada. Tell it how many billions of dollars it is costing the taxpayer simply because of some crazed, Thatcherite-like monetary attack on the economy."
As people scream and beg for mercy across this country, it does not matter whether you are talking about farmers, small business people, people in medium-sized firms, international business people are laughing at us. They go back to their host countries and borrow money for next to nothing. Our Canadian businesses cannot get access to capital because we are drawing in money through an artificially high rate to pay off our debt.
I cannot think of a situation any more more incompetent than the federal government welcoming offshore capital to finance our debt. For generations we financed ourselves, although we might have begrudged it. We were able to do that through the Canadian Savings Bond program and other short-term treasury notes processes.

A few years ago the federal government very quietly gave up financing the debt within the country. Now we are borrowing offshore, which contributes to the depletion of our national savings. Canadians are saying two things as they hear this debate taking place. They are saying: "Keep up the fight on taxes. Keep up the fight against borrowing. Tell the government in no uncertain terms that we do not want to continue in this fashion any longer."
A Winnipeg journalist writing in the Winnipeg Free Press spent some time elaborating on one of the missing links in the Canadian taxation system. Many people talk about tax reform, which is one of the more over-used expressions in political debate lately. This government took on "tax reform".
What does it mean to have tax reform when you are a Tory? It means you decrease the amount of money you tax in the corporate sector and you increase the amount of money you are taking from average Canadians.
For example, since 1985, the year after the Tories took power, personal income taxes have risen 49 per cent, and sales taxes have gone up 51 per cent. Meanwhile, corporate taxes have actually dropped 10 per cent. According to Frances Russell, the columnist at the Winnipeg Free Press, had the Mulroney government maintained the same ratio of corporate taxes to corporate profit existing in 1984, it would have taken in an additional $6 billion. She is basing her writing on a Dalhousie University economist, Allistair Sinclair, who noted that this extra tax revenue would, in turn, have reduced interest charges by another $2 billion, leaving a deficit of $22 billion rather than the current $30 billion.
Canada's poorest taxpayers saw their bracket climb from 9 per cent to 17 per cent. Meanwhile, Canada's wealthiest citizens watched their bracket drop from 34 per cent to 29 per cent. That 29 per cent begins at the $55,000 level, meaning that the tax system treats multimillionaires and middle-class income earners the same.
When people read this sort of information about the Canadian tax system, they begin to have a sense of disbelief within themselves. How can you have a system when, at the time this government took over, it said that the biggest problem facing it was the fact that the Liberals had bankrupted the country? What was the government going to do? It was going to tell all its
