friends in the high-income brackets not to worry because their taxes were going to be reduced; but, by the way, the rest of you Canadians watch out because we are going to take it from you. That turns out to be one of the meanest and most miserable governmental strategies we have ever seen in this country, and perhaps even in the western world in the last five years.
Nobody has really sat down and thought about how many tax increases have been introduced since this government took over.
In round one, in 1985, there was an extra two cents per litre for gasoline, and an additional 25 cents per package of 25 cigarettes. There was a 2 per cent increase in the excise tax on wine, beer and other alcoholic beverages. The federal sales tax rose one percentage point and was extended to candy, pet food, soft drinks, shampoos, soaps, some energy-saving devices and insulation materials. A surtax of up to 10 per cent was imposed on middle and upper-income earners for the next 18 months. That was only round one.
In round two, in 1986, a surtax boosted income tax by 1.5 per cent in 1986, and 3 per cent more starting in 1987. The government likes to introduce taxes, give you 12 months to forget about it, and then hit you. The federal sales tax increased by another percentage point. The excise tax rose by 6 per cent on tobacco and 4 per cent on alcohol. An estimated four million low-income families received refundable tax credits of up to $50 per adult and $25 per child to help offset the impact of the higher sales taxes.
In round three, in 1987, excise taxes on gasoline and diesel fuel increased by one cent a litre. Thxes on cigarettes and other tobacco products went up 4 per cent, resulting in a three-cent increase in a package of 25. A federal sales tax of 12 per cent was added to snack foods such as popcorn, potato chips, and granola bars, pop-sicles and some types of ice-cream. Even the granola crowd was hit. Airline passengers faced a new $4 tax on domestic flights and on tickets purchased abroad to help pay for measures such as increased security.
The most interesting is round four. In round four there is only one tax increase. That was an extra one-cent a
litre tax on gasoline and aviation fuel, with a corresponding 1 per cent rebate for farmers and fishermen.
What was the year for round four? The year was 1988. What else took place in 1988? Was that not the year of a federal election? What a coincidence.
In round five we are now back up to speed. There is the proposed goods and services tax which is now 7 per cent, but who knows what it will be when these guys get finished with it?
Second, there are personal income tax increases. The federal surtax on all taxpayers went to 5 per cent from 3 per cent. An additional 3 per cent surtax was slapped on people with incomes above $70,000. There were corporate tax increases of 7.1 per cent. There was the so-called clawback of baby bonus and old age security benefits from those with net annual income of more than $50,000. The federal sales tax rose to 13.5 per cent from 12 per cent. The excise tax went up 2 cents a litre on unleaded gasoline-what people were touting as being a great environmental benefit. There is also a 3-cent increase on leaded gasoline. Excise tax on tobacco rose, including a $4 a carton increase. Sales tax rose to 19 per cent from 18 per cent on alcohol, to 9 per cent from 8 per cent on construction materials and to 13.5 per cent from 12 per cent on telecommunications and programming services.
Can you imagine that as a record? When I look at 1990 and 1991 I fear for Canadians and what other burdens they are going to be carrying. With some of these taxes we lose sight of just how much money the government has gained as a result of these tax increases.
Let us talk about some of them. When the government eliminated the registered home ownership savings plan in 1985 it received another $105 million. Did it have any idea how much difficulty it brought to families, particularly families in the Toronto, Calgary and Vancouver markets by eliminating that opportunity that these young families had to save for their first home? It probably have no idea. On the changes to marital exemptions it pick up another $20 million. The elimination of low income federal tax reductions brought in $650 million. The temporary 5 per cent and 10 per cent surtax in 1985 accounted for another $500 million. The de-indexation of tax brackets and family allowances and tax credits in 1986 accounted for another $635 million. The permanent general 3 per cent surtax in 1986 brought in another $1.2 billion. The family allowance and old age security clawback in 1989 accounted for another $500 million. The

general surtax increases from 3 per cent, pro-rated and beginning in 1990 brought in $1.1 billion. The high income surtax was pro-rated for 1989 and increased a full 3 per cent in January for $165 million. The list goes on and on. It is endless as to the amount of money this government has collected from Canadians.
What is the end product for us sitting here? It wants us to approve another borrowing bill for $25.5 billion. The questions that are being asked throughout this country and in Winnipeg North Centre are these. When is this going to end? When is some sanity going to be brought to the government? When is it going to be stopped from taxing and from borrowing? When is it going to start taking care of us again?

Mr. Speaker, when one speaks of the poor in this country one does not know where to begin nowadays. You do not know whether you should just talk about the increased difficulty of students who had an extra 3 per cent surcharge on their loans for administration. You ask yourself why would you begin to tax the poorest people for giving them the opportunity. Can you imagine a welfare office charging people for the right to receive money? This is what this government is doing. It is saying: "If you are so poor you have to borrow money to go to school. In order to get the money you have to pay us 3 per cent". If you saw that taking place in the bank among the poorest people in the country there would be a revolt. This government hiding behind its Prime Minister and all its sanctimony says: "That is fine. That is what it costs to administer it. That is all there is to it".
Where do we begin to talk about native peoples in a short answer and their poverty? With this government's new strategy, as announced through the Secretary of State, who does not seem to understand what he has done, they cannot even communicate with each other.

They cannot even build up within themselves the communication infrastructure so that Canadians understand the desperate situation they are in and that they can share from one part of the country to the other what they are doing. They do not get on a plane every day. They are not like the business traveller. These are people who are trying to understand each other's situation, develop some commonality of spirit among the 300,000 to 500,000 aboriginal peoples in this country. Yet we turn around in a moment of need, right in the middle of judicial inquiries saying how unfairly they have been treated and we say to them, by the way we are taking away your money to communicate. Best of luck to you. It is that sort of attitude which brings a total amount of disrepute to the government.
It is not only the opposition party that feels this. The Canadian Council on Social Development responded to the budget with the following statement: "If we have had eight consecutive years of economic growth, why is this the sixth consecutive year we have had cuts in social programs?"
I think that is the critical question. Why, after all this growth? We know the Prime Minister loves to talk about his jobs, jobs, jobs. But does he talk about the heartache he has created by cut-backs, cut-backs, cut-backs? I do not hear anything. Does anybody else hear anything? The answer is no.
For these reasons, and the question about what has happened to the poor in this country gets to the heart of our opposition to this borrowing bill.

Mr. Speaker, any debate on borrowing authority is an opportunity to talk about a great many things and I hope that I will have an opportunity to touch on a number of policy areas in the course of my remarks.
Today, in Question Period when the hon. member for Nickel Belt got up I felt that we had a very convenient summary, if you like, of the political landscape in Canada. As you know the hon. member for Nickel Belt has been on a weekly basis every Wednesday awarding the corporate welfare bum of the week award to a corporation selected from among three that are nomi-

nated every Wednesday and these corporations invariably have similar characteristics. They are large, they pay no taxes but also as it turns out in many cases, although they are not able to pay taxes by the government's definition, they are too poor to pay taxes, even though many of them make millions of dollars in profits, they are able to make donations to the Conservative and Liberal parties of Canada. This surely must be a sign to all of those who want to hear, those who have ears and can hear, of what is really at the root of our Canadian political system. The corporate sector is looked after regardless of who is in government, whether it be the Liberal party as it was for so many years, or the Conservative party.
That is why we found in recent weeks that the opposition of the Liberal party to the goods and services tax has been rather pro forma, that they have sought to dissociate themselves from the authenticity and the tenacity of the NDP opposition to the goods and services tax because these are people who know that the goods and services tax is part of the corporate agenda and who know that if the Tories did not implement it that should they be elected next time around that it is the sort of thing that they also would have to do in obedience to the same masters. So we find that there is this funny sort of reticence about digging themselves too deep with respect to the goods and services tax, hoping that they can get away with being seen to be strongly in opposition to it but also hoping that the government very much succeeds in getting it through.
Of course the story of the Conservative Party in government from 1984 to 1992 or 1993, whenever it comes to a well deserved end, will be that it will have done the dirty work of the Liberal Party of Canada. It will have done what the right wing of the Liberal Party of Canada would have wanted to do but may have found it more difficult than the Tories have done. To be fair to the Liberals, what they would do shamefacedly and evasively, Conservative always do with enthusiasm. That makes them in some respects more worthy opponents, but it also makes them more destructive because they do not know restraint in their policies.
The fact of the matter is that the middle class, the low and middle income earners in Canada are under attack from every which way one can think of as a result of the
tax and social policies of the government. People are starting to catch on that they under attack. People are starting to catch on that it is getting harder and harder to make ends meet. Everywhere they turn they are met by an increase in something, generally a tax or a price, or a decrease in something, generally a benefit or service of some kind. People are only going to put up with this for so long. It is unfortunate that in the nature of the Canadian political system they may well have to choose once again between tweedledum and tweedledee, between trying to eat their soup with a knife or a fork, leaving the spoon untried.
One of the other things I would like to talk about is the whole question of the transportation policy in the country. It is something that I do not get to talk about as much as I used to being the external affairs critic for my party. Transportation policy in the country is very important and very important to people in my riding. I can think of a number of different things that are of concern, but perhaps I will start with the one which has had the highest profile since the last election. That of course is the cuts to VIA Rail. It seems to me that the cuts to VIA Rail sum up and are a rather depressing symbol of everything that is wrong with the policy of the government.
There is a train which since the 1920s, and perhaps even before that, has served many people in my riding. They are the cottagers who have cottages along the CNR mainline in places like Ophir, Winnitoba, Rice Lake, Malachi and Ottermere. For years people have been going down to their cottages on the train. There was a special train called the "Camper Special" which went down on Friday night and came back on Sunday night. In the early 1980s, as a result of negotiations between VIA and the campers, this service was blended into the Winnipeg to Capreol service. The train was scheduled in such a way that it could meet the needs of the cottagers.
When the former transport minister, the hon. member for Roberval, ordered VIA to come up with a plan to implement cuts, he ordered them to preserve service on nine remote routes. One of those routes was the Winnipeg to Capreol route. Eight out of the nine routes were indeed preserved, but the ninth, the Winnipeg to Capreol route, was subsumed or absorbed into the transcontinental service which was to run from Vancouver to Winnipeg and from Winnipeg east over the CN mainline,

which is where the Winnipeg to Capreol service used to be.
That train now leaves on Saturday night at 8:15 and conies back on Monday morning at 7. That is bad enough, but the fact is that VIA has indicated it has no intention of adding any equipment to that train to service the needs of the cottagers. For instance, take the long weekend in May. On any long weekend in May for the last 60 years that train has probably taken anywhere between 500 and 700 people down to the lake. Do you know how many coach seats there are on that train for the long weekend in May, Mr. Speaker? Fifty-six seats. Maybe that is all they will need because who is going to want to go down on Saturday night of the long weekend and come back on Monday morning of the long weekend?
That is not preserving service to that remote area. Many of these areas have no roads. How are they supposed to get to their cottage? That is the situation that people find themselves in because of the policy of this government. What are we going to have to do eventually, unless the government comes to its senses? All these hundreds of people who formerly took a train to their cottage in two hours will now travel on the Trans-Canada Highway between Winnipeg and Kenora.
Then we are going to have to cut new roads through the bush, in some cases through wilderness areas. We are going to put more hydrocarbons into the air and clog up the Trans-Canada Highway which is already clogged with trucks, thanks to the deregulation policies of this government which has taken freight off the railway tracks and put it on the highways.
Next we are going to cut roads through bush that up until now has been undisturbed. On the roads that do exist, some of them into adjoining lakes, people will need to have pick-up trucks or four by fours in order to have half a chance of ever getting out again, once they get in. Other people will have to go seven and a half miles across water to get to their cottage.
All this is in the name of a phoney way of keeping the books, because all this is bookkeeping. All this is policy set on keeping one set of books, the VIA set of books with respect to that particular service and not figuring into the larger bookkeeping the cost of more hydrocarbons going into the atmosphere, the safety matter of

having more people on the highways, and the environmental factor of having to cut roads through areas that up until now have been left alone, not to mention the enormous inconvenience to families and communities which had a right to expect that this service which has been provided since the very beginning, if you like, would continue pursuant to the orders of the Minister of Transport himself who said that service to remote communities should be preserved.
I have spoken to the former Minister of Transport and the current Minister of Transport. I have not given up that we may yet find some solution to this problem. I think that part of the reason why, so far, some of the people are not as upset as they will be, come the long weekend in May, is because they cannot believe that anybody would do this. They think: "You've got to be kidding that I won't be able to get to my cottage". They cannot believe that they will not be able to get to their cottages that, in some cases, has been there for three or four generations.

This government is committed to subsidies, subsidies of the rich and the rest of the country has to pay for the kinds of subsidies they have been arranging, like the $500,000 capital gains tax exemption. If that is not a subsidy, I do not know what the hell is.
I am running out of time. I had hoped to talk about health care. I had hoped to talk about UIC. I even hoped to talk about foreign policy. But I have this feeling that I will not because I got talking about transportation.
While I am at it, Mr. Speaker, I would not mind passing on to you and hopefully to the Ministry of Transport and the National Transportation Agency what I have been picking up from people in my riding who work on the railway, and that is as a result of the policy of deregulation we see a decrease in maintenance. I invite you, Mr. Speaker, sometime when you are in your riding, now that the weather is improving, to sit by the level crossing with your window down and listen to the flat wheels going by. The railway has a policy of not "bad ordering" wheels the way they used to. One of the reasons they do not is because they do not have as many carmen inspecting the wheels as they used to. These trains are going bang, bang, bang, bang all the way down.
People who know anything about railways know that this is happening because all you have to do is listen if you have a trained ear. That is what is happening. I have people who work on the railway, and others who are writing to me about this. They know that maintenance is being neglected as a result of deregulation.
They know that at Symington Yard at the Hump, where they hump cars and send them down different tracks and marshall different trains that they have taken out what are called the manual car retards, the way that guys used to be able to judge cars: their weight, what kind of car they were, the right speed, et cetera, and respond accordingly. They have taken those out. Now they do everything by computer. If you stand by the hump you can hear these cars, some of them with
hazardous commodities in them, going bang, bang, bang. There are people I know in the railway who live near there who are moving out. They know it is only a matter of time before something happens, thanks to the great computer that is supposed to look after everything, as in so many other instances in society where we are removing people and replacing them with these little terminals that are supposed to do everything. Black boxes on the ends of trains. Every time I see a train go by and there is no caboose, I realize just how little we have succeeded in trying to resist the agenda of this government.
It goes on and on. In Ontario, the government is talking about double and triple trailers on trucks. Pretty soon you will not want to go on the highway unless you are in a tank for fear of colliding with one of these things. The rail beds will be increasingly empty. The next step, once the Tories get their way, once they get the successor to the Crow payment paid not to the railways but to the producers, we will be trucking grain all over the place. There will hardly be anything to put on the railway. The highways will be even more clogged, in this case with trucks hauling grain to bigger and bigger terminals owned by Cargill and other multinational agri-business people who are trying to arrange the world economy to their own benefit and to hell with communities, to hell with workers and to hell with everything that the Conservatives used to say they were for: small town Canada, rural values, all that sort of thing where people are not subject to urban rot. These are the people who are destroying rural Canada, their post offices, branchlines, elevators, you name it, all in the name of global competitiveness. It is disgraceful.
